15.3 · Stopping an owned tree/group never includes a process with conflicting or unestablished ownership, and the covered membership is stated.
15.4 · A bounded initial stop and, under C1, forced escalation are each followed by checks of the root and covered children; a surviving child prevents a stopped result.
15.5 · A live or unconfirmed survivor keeps its record and makes the stop unsuccessful, regardless of whether the operating system accepted the signal.
15.6 · Multiple named targets each receive an outcome, and any refusal or survivor makes the overall result unsuccessful.

capabilities.title: 16 · Finish with an honest inventory
capabilities.description:
The session can clear records of work confirmed gone without hiding work that may still be running. Its closing check distinguishes an empty observed inventory from an incomplete observation, so a tidy record cannot become a false claim that the computer is idle.

As built: `@storytree/processes/closing` and `@storytree/processes` export `clearOwned({ owner, home?, knownGaps? })`, `readClosing({ home?, owner?, knownGaps?, shared? })` and `renderClosing(reading)`. Clear removes only the caller session/harness's records, with named subagents limited to their own records; delegated sessions' records are untouched. Original lifetimes and all registered descendants must be confirmed gone. Live, unknown and foreign records remain; unreadable records and known gaps prevent unproved child clearance. Removal failures are reported separately from successful removals.

Clear rereads records and child membership after probing and before unlinking. Changed, disappearing, reparented or newly registered children retain the affected parent; only this call's confirmed removals may shrink its previously observed membership. It preserves request evidence and gap records, never signals processes, and changes neither claims, sessions nor increments.

The closing reading reuses the listing API in all-session scope, irrespective of the caller, session end or released claims. Its status is `empty`, `remaining` or `incomplete`. Live/unknown rows stay visible; persisted read/registration gaps and caller-carried gaps whose persistence failed make it incomplete and name missing evidence separately. An empty verdict says “no tracked session work remains on this machine”, with the launch coverage and an explicit remote-machine limit. Shared work remains separately visible and is never stopped automatically.

These are point-in-time observations, without a launch interlock. Only explicitly registered descendants are covered; neither whole-machine idleness nor remote clearance is claimed. Evidence: `packages/processes/evidence/closing/README.md`, `red.txt`, `red-membership.txt`, `green.txt`, `gate.txt`, and the PR's three native CI checks. As built (installed clear doors): storytree processes clear and MCP clear_own_runs call clearOwned without signalling, preserve removed, retained, failed and gaps as separate fields, then return an all-session readClosing. Read gaps from clear are carried as knownGaps into that closing reading. Failed removals or clear gaps exit nonzero / set MCP isError while retaining the full result. Remaining live work and unknown shared app identity remain visible in the closing verdict; clear success does not claim closure or whole-computer idleness. The current doors perform no launches and have no additional unpersisted launch-gap source. Evidence: packages/processes/evidence/doors2/.

contracts.title: 16.1 · Clear removes only the caller's records whose original processes and covered children are confirmed gone, leaving every other session's records untouched.
16.2 · Clear retains live, unknown and unreadable records and reports failed removals rather than claiming they disappeared.
16.3 · The closing reading cannot say that no owned work remains while live or unknown work survives, even if the session has ended or its claims have been released.
16.4 · A known registration/read gap makes the closing reading incomplete under G1, with the missing evidence named separately from known live work.
16.5 · An empty closing reading says “no tracked session work remains on this machine” with its coverage, and never claims a whole-machine census or remote-machine clearance.

capabilities.title: 11 · Machines
capabilities.description: The computers that work on a project, each with a short name its owner gives it, its hostname and its id, read from what the trunks and machine.json already hold; a way to give this computer its name and to ask which one it is; and the sessions list showing each session's machine by that name.

contracts.title: 11.1 · `storytree machine name <name>` gives this computer a short name, kept with its hostname and id; a name another machine has, or one that is not a short name, is refused
11.2 · `storytree machine list` shows the project's machines, each with its name, hostname and id, and marks this one; `storytree machine this` says which one this computer is
11.3 · The sessions list shows each session's machine by its short name, or by its hostname while it has none
11.4 · An increment's machine is checked against Machines: a named machine is kept, "none" clears it, and any other name is refused naming the known ones

11.5 · On Linux, machine health reads the boot time, MemAvailable, the 15-minute load and the root disk, and names a concern for memory under its limit, load over it and a disk fuller than it, or a reading it could not take

11.6 · On Windows, machine health reads the boot time, the memory available, the processor queue and the system drive, and names a concern for each past its limit, or a queue PowerShell could not give
11.7 · `storytree machine health` reads the machine against the limits in settings: concerns come first and refuse, so the command exits 1, and a healthy machine answers with each reading

capabilities.title: 17 · Friction
capabilities.description: Every session files what fought it (friction) and the owner's redirections (re-steers), with evidence; a landing drains the open reports and routes each to its remedy with a reason. Its verbs (the friction and resteer families, and the record_friction, reinforce, record_resteer, friction_drain and route tools) are declared once here and mounted by both doors.

contracts.title: 17.1 · Friction with vague evidence is refused.
17.2 · A re-steer whose evidence is a paraphrase is refused.
17.3 · `reinforce` adds a dated recurrence, keeping the route of a routed report (a resolved or dismissed one reopens, ADR-1016 D2).

17.4 · It records friction with concrete evidence and a re-steer with the owner's quoted words, the agent's account kept apart; friction whose evidence is vague prose, a re-steer whose evidence quotes nobody, and a defect with no failure mode are each refused as a readable answer, and nothing is written. Shared capture stamps the calling branch and UTC date, and refuses a fourth friction report on that branch that day, counting routed reports too; the refusal names the cap and points to friction reinforce.

17.5 · Reinforcing friction through the tool or public capture function appends dated concrete evidence to the same item and preserves the route of a routed one (a resolved or dismissed one reopens, ADR-1016 D2). Invalid recurrences write nothing.

17.6 · The daily friction cap counts each writer's own reports: on a branch every session shares, a second session's report is accepted after another filed three that day, and each is still refused its own fourth; a report whose writer was not recorded counts toward every writer's three

17.7 · A re-steer whose evidence is the user's exact words without quotation marks is refused naming the step that passes, putting those words inside double quotation marks, and the same words inside them are then recorded

17.8 · The friction drain holds at most three open friction reports (ADR-1016 D1) that another session filed, never one filed from the session's own branch. Reports with the most recurrences come first, with oldest first on ties; no recurrences counts as zero, and missing provenance still counts as another session's report.

17.9 · route(friction, route, reason, options?) records the routing judgement with its reason and an optional dischargedBy reference to the remedy that landed. The reference is trimmed and must be non-empty when supplied; omitting it preserves an existing stamp. An already-routed report can receive its stamp later. A route with no reason or a blank delivery reference is refused without writing.

17.10 · A tool route requires a live, non-closed increment whose remedies names this friction, unless the report already carries a delivered-by stamp or receives one in this call. An unrelated or closed increment is insufficient; refusal writes nothing and explains the missing remedy or delivery reference.

17.11 · A report already routed is routed again only to the same route (a later delivery stamp or a clearer reason); routing it elsewhere is refused naming the earlier route and its reason, and nothing is written, so two librarian passes cannot silently replace each other's judgement.

17.12 · Every route but nothing needs a live, non-closed increment whose remedies names the report, or a delivery stamp given now or already carried; refused otherwise with nothing written. The drain lists open reports, so one reopened is offered again and may be routed afresh

17.13 · The friction drain leases the reports it lists to the session that asked, for a few minutes; a second session draining in that window is handed the next unleased reports, not the same ones, and a lease ends when the report is routed or the lease lapses
17.14 · route() checks whether a report is already routed inside its write, not before it, so two passes racing to route one report two ways write one route and refuse the other

17.15 · `friction route <friction> --to <route> --reason …` records the route and reason, with an optional --discharged-by stamp; its refusals (a tool route with no live remedy) reach the caller unchanged and write nothing (ADR-0789 D2).
17.16 · `friction drain` lists the friction drain for the calling branch: up to three unrouted reports other branches filed, most recurrences first (ADR-0789 D2).
17.17 · Session management declares the `friction` and `resteer` families the command line lists 13th and 14th: friction filed on one branch, with its links and the writer, is drained on another

17.18 · Session management declares its friction tools once, and the MCP server serves them from its declarations: record_friction, reinforce, record_resteer, friction_drain and route; a capture refusal answers as a refusal with nothing written
17.19 · Friction marked about storytree answers with a pre-filled GitHub issue draft for the user to review and submit, the paths and project name stripped; storytree sends nothing

capabilities.title: 18 · Scheduled processes
capabilities.description: The runner's two commands: which scheduled process records are due now, and recording that one ran with its outcome, so a factory's routines are run when their schedule comes round.

contracts.title: 18.1 · A scheduled process is due once its schedule comes round after its latest run, unless its time is past its grace or its precheck finds nothing to do
18.2 · A recorded run stops a process being due, and its outcome reads back; missed and skipped are recorded only when still so
18.3 · A plugin librarian's run is listed due on its trigger

18.4 · A process with the precheck questions-to-prep is due only while an open question on an active arc has no prep mark or was edited after it, or a settled question that carries a would-be answer is unscored; with none, its run is recorded skipped

capabilities.title: 19 · Worktree setup
capabilities.description: Right after storytree makes a worktree in a user's project, or a Codex session attaches the one its app just made, it runs the setup the project's own untracked local file names (.storytree/worktree.local.json): setup commands, gitignored files copied from the main checkout, and folders shared from it, so the agent never starts in an empty checkout. A team's checked-in .storytree/worktree.json, with the same keys, is read beside it, the local file winning key by key; its setup and teardown commands run only once the user has approved that exact set at their own terminal (`storytree workspace approve-setup <fingerprint>`, kept per repository in their settings), are asked again when they change, and are skipped with a reason, never blocking the worktree, when an agent runs alone. The file's teardown commands run, in a process of their own, when the reaper is about to remove a worktree set up this way.

contracts.title: 19.1 · A workspace made in a project whose untracked `.storytree/worktree.local.json` names setup commands, files to copy and folders to share runs each command in the new worktree, copies each file or folder from the main checkout and shares each folder (a junction on Windows), and its answer reports each step

19.2 · A setup step that fails (a command exiting non-zero, a path with `..`, an absolute path or a link leading out of the repository, a path git does not ignore, a missing source, a copy over the cap, or a local file git tracks or cannot parse) is reported naming why, the rest still run, and the claim and the worktree are kept
19.3 · A workspace made in a project with no `.storytree/worktree.local.json` is made exactly as before: nothing is run, copied or shared, and its answer reports no setup

19.4 · A worktree set up from the local file that names teardown commands has them run in it, in order, by a process of their own once the reaper would remove it, and is removed on a later pass once they have finished, a failed one included; a worktree never set up runs none

19.5 · A Codex session attaching the worktree its app just made at the prepared commit has it set up from the local file, reported in the attach's answer, and set up once however often it attaches; a Claude Code session attaching its own worktree runs no setup

19.6 · A checked-in `.storytree/worktree.json` is read beside the local file, the local file winning key by key, and its setup and teardown commands run only once the user has approved that exact set: before then, or after they change, the workspace is made without them and its answer names the command that approves them

19.7 · `storytree workspace approve-setup <fingerprint>` records the user's approval of the checked-in setup's commands only from a person at their own terminal, and is refused, recording nothing, when the fingerprint is not the checked-in file's current one

19.8 · When an agent runs alone (its harness says no one is attending), an unapproved checked-in setup's commands are skipped and the workspace's answer says no one is here to approve them, rather than asking

capabilities.title: 1 · Lifecycle
capabilities.description: When the app opens it starts the database that holds every project's library, and it keeps it running until the app is quit: closing the window leaves both running in the background, with a tray icon whose Quit stops them, so agents' work is still recorded. The app can also be controlled from outside (ADR-0656 D0): asking it to quit from the command line stops it as the tray's Quit does. There is one owner at a time: opening the app again brings its window forward, another program holding the database is named, and while it runs the app leaves records saying where the database is and how to open the app, which is how an agent's session finds it or opens it.

dependsOn.title: 2 · A server on a data directory

contracts.title: 2.1 · A cluster is made only where there is none, asking every connection for the installation's password and listening on 127.0.0.1 only; a directory holding anything else is refused and left untouched.
2.2 · A started server answers SELECT 1 at the url handed back; stop stops it, a second stop is harmless, and it can be started again, on a port asked for.
2.3 · A start on a data directory a live process holds is refused with a DataDirInUseError naming that process and its owner, and the holder's server is left running.
2.4 · A server left running by a process that died is stopped and replaced, and a dead owner's record alone is cleared, so the start goes ahead.

2.5 · A start can carry server settings for that run, as the throwaway test server runs with fsync, synchronous commit and full-page writes off; a start without them keeps the cluster's own, and a setting that is not one plain word is refused before anything starts.
2.6 · The server lets in only a client with the installation's password, which it hands over privately while it runs
2.7 · A cluster made when local connections were trusted is given the password before its server starts again, keeping its data, and an interrupted start never reopens it
2.8 · Clients sign in as an ordinary role that owns storytree's databases, never as the superuser
2.9 · A throwaway test server can hand back the superuser's url beside its client's, for tests' setup, while its clients and handoff stay the ordinary role

2.10 · On Windows the sign-in is kept private beside a data directory whose folder lets this user change files but not take ownership (a checkout under C:\code): the access list is set without asking to change an owner the user already is
2.11 · On Windows a sign-in folder a failed first run left behind is made private before any sign-in goes into it

2.14 · Run as root (a cloud container), the Postgres tools and the server run as the unprivileged account nobody, which is handed the cluster, the server log and initdb's password file and let through the folders above them; run as anyone else they run as that user
2.15 · A database an interrupted run left invalid is dropped when the server next starts, saying so once, so it can be made again and connected to
1.6 · With storytree closed, an agent's session start opens it: the installed app where there is one, never a development copy in its place.

1.7 · Closing the window leaves the app and its database running; the tray's Quit, or asking the app to quit from outside (`storytree app quit`), stops them: it stops the database once, and the app exits only after it has stopped. Quitting, including smoke teardown and restarting into an update, stops the page's polling before closing the library, without logging a closed-library error.

1.8 · Each project gets a snapshot in `~/.storytree/0.3/backups/<project>/` once a day, keeping that project's newest 14 (ADR-0641 B1): when the app starts it takes one of each project whose newest successful snapshot is missing or a day old and reuses one under a day old, and while it runs it takes the next at each project's day mark; a failed or partial snapshot does not count. A snapshot is one JSON object written a line per record and history entry, never built as one string, so a project past JavaScript's longest string (about 512 MB) is still backed up, and `readBackup` reads a file back line by line as the object `restore` takes. On POSIX, backup directories are private (0700) and partial and published snapshots are owner-readable and writable only (0600), independent of umask or an existing traversable application home. Startup and direct backups repair retained snapshot and partial permissions, including those of removed projects, before reuse; unrelated files keep their contents and modes. On Windows, backup directories and retained snapshots have protected DACLs granting only the current user access, and each partial is created exclusively with that DACL before snapshot bytes are written. Retained permissions are repaired before freshness reuse; a permission failure writes no new snapshot and prevents reuse. Unrelated home files and unrelated children keep their permissions and contents. Effective-access tests on Windows exclude an unrelated non-administrative identity even under permissive inherited and explicit ACLs; privileged administrator override is outside this promise.
1.9 · With the library set to Cloud SQL, the app starts no local Postgres and opens its projects, surfaces and snapshots on the instance; quitting leaves the instance alone.

1.10 · With the library set to Cloud SQL and the instance unreachable (no Google sign-in, a refused account, or no answer in time), the window says so in the refusal's own words and what to fix, and the app never falls back to the local library.

1.11 · With the library on Cloud SQL, where the app starts no local database, the running app is still found (its launch record carries its process id): storytree app quit quits it, a stopped app reads as not running, and a delivery waits for the app itself rather than for a database it never starts.

1.12 · The installed app opens at sign-in, straight to the tray with no window, unless the user has turned that off in the gear's Updates section; a development copy or a portable build never registers itself
1.13 · A start that fails ends the app instead of lingering half-started
1.14 · The window keeps drawing through the machine's GPU resets: repeated GPU process crashes never block the app from WebGL, so a lost globe is restored instead of staying white until a restart
1.15 · Started with --callback-check, the app reports each sign-in callback a later start hands it, and whether it reached the sign-in session, without opening a window or its library
1.16 · A page operation a story declares reaches that story's answer in the main process, with the page's arguments

1.17 · The tray, the window and the packaged app wear the mark: the tray and window in the night colourway on a dark taskbar and the day colourway otherwise, following a change while running; the installer and app bundle in the day colourway

1.18 · A story's page operations its package's manifest names are answered in the main process and offered to the page, with neither main.ts nor bridge.ts naming the story to mount it (the page's type may still name its bridge, ADR-1030 D3)
1.19 · The page's errors reach app.log

1.20 · The desktop app answers no page operation of a story part switched off on this computer: each of its channels refuses, saying the part is off and how to switch it on, and every other part's operations are answered
1.21 · A page title change reaching a destroyed window is ignored, never an uncaught error; a live window gets the title with the build
1.22 · The main process's uncaught errors reach app.log
1.23 · After a logged main-process error, the app offers Keep going or Restart
1.24 · A factory plugin standing in for a switched-off part answers its page operations and serves its views in the part's place
1.25 · Each uncaught main-process exception and unhandled rejection is one record in the user's own library; a repeat adds to its count
1.26 · When the library cannot take a main-process error, app.log keeps it and nothing more is raised
1.27 · A second start, the dock's activate or the tray brings the window back, opening it again if it was closed; none reaches a destroyed window, and none opens one while the app is quitting
1.28 · The window's page never navigates away or opens another window, and the window shows itself once ready unless the app runs headless; a window destroyed first is left alone
1.29 · The page's reads and project choice, asked before the library opens, get no projects or are refused saying it is not open; once it opens, or reopens, each is answered by the library open then

1.30 · Started with --smoke, the app exits red on any main-process error, one raised while it quits included, after closing, reopening and quitting its window at awkward moments, and never waits on an error box

1.31 · While the user's library holds an app error not yet marked submitted, the app asks on opening to have their agent submit a GitHub issue, and stops asking once it is marked submitted from that box

1.32 · After five restarts in a row the app stops restarting itself, on every channel, keeps running its build, and records the stop as an error the user is asked to report; a start that stays up 30 minutes resets the count
1.33 · A start writes each timing mark once to app.log, as milliseconds from launch
1.34 · Everything the app says is kept in app.log in its home, which stays bounded
1.35 · The window's session grants only writing plain text to the clipboard, and refuses every other web permission request and check

1.36 · Started with --smoke, the app prints a smoke: line as each phase starts, keeps Electron's files in a scratch folder of its own so an open app's folder cannot hold it, and a run that gives up names the phase it was stuck in

1.37 · The desktop app composes the project records its story packages' manifests name, bundled and unbundled (none in base since code review's QA ledger became a factory plugin's, ADR-1209), and the setup help's Delete forgets them with a project, but a switched-off part's
1.38 · A main-side failure reaches the page in its own words
1.39 · The app takes its flags only from a start with no sign-in link, before '--', its developer flags only in development or CI, and no network or device path for a screenshot
1.40 · An unreachable library is said once per outage, not a stack per poll
1.41 · The page and its files are served from the app's own scheme, never file://, and a page-check start proves the page loads and its road worker answers
1.42 · The app opens its projects with the kinds of record its mounted factory plugins declare
1.43 · Quitting stops the journey, then the page reads, then the library, then Postgres, once however often it is asked; a part that fails to stop is said and the next stops all the same
1.44 · The app restarts itself only while it is not stopping, asked again after the seed check, no seed is being written to its own Postgres, and no backup holds it
1.45 · A library whose data folder another program holds is said as in use by that program, or another program, with its process and what to do; any other failure says why it could not be opened

1.46 · The main process bundles into one file for Electron that loads nothing from outside it but Node's own modules, Electron and the optional modules it never loads or loads lazily, so a packaged app needs no node_modules
1.47 · The preload script, bundled as the app bundles it, gives the page the bridge as `storytree` and nothing else, with the main process's answers on sign-in for feedback and stand-ins

1.48 · The main process and preload bundles pack each #parts/<kind> from the parts list Plugin loader's step writes, as part of that build, for the importing file's package, in its order with each part's owner and the host's parts graph; a bundle whose list is missing, or out of date with a package.json it was written from, or that imports a kind its package.json maps no list for, fails naming it rather than pack the wrong parts

capabilities.title: 2 · Storytree projects
capabilities.description: The app lists the storytree projects in its database and shows one at a time. Its always-visible, full-width top app bar holds only a gear at the right. The gear opens a large centred overlay with Projects, Settings, Updates and Help sections. Projects moves the whole app to another project in place; Settings mounts the agent link's per-user panel, Updates mounts the app's existing update status, and Help mounts app-setup's existing help surface. The separate arcs-only bar sits below the app bar and the forest starts below both. This capability also decides which project is on show when the app opens.

contracts.title: 2.1 · The app bar's Projects tab lists every product, with the one on show selected. Choosing another project switches the forest; a failed choice shows its reason beside the tabs, keeps the project on show selected, and leaves the tabs available for retry.
2.2 · The list is read again every three seconds, including while empty; a first project appears without restarting, unchanged reads leave the surface alone, and closing the page stops polling.

2.3 · Reopening follows the latest successful explicit project choice, whether made in the picker or by saying yes to setup. A newer picker choice supersedes an older setup choice, and a newer setup choice supersedes an older picker choice. `--project` wins on launch and becomes the remembered choice when that project exists. A remembered project that has gone falls back to the first; an unknown explicit project is named as missing.

2.4 · After a successful setup yes, the chosen project is durably recorded and becomes the project on show on the next refresh, or on reopening. The last successfully recorded yes wins even when several setups complete between reads or while the window is closed. A project-list read never overwrites an explicit choice, including one recorded while that read is in flight; discovering a name alone does not count as choosing it (ADR-0657 D3).
2.5 · With no projects, the app tells the user to add a folder as a project with New project… in the project list at the top left, or run `storytree doctor --set-up <name>` in the folder.

2.6 · The gear opens a full-size centred overlay below the always-visible app bar, with space around it at wide and narrow window sizes. Clicking the gear again, pressing Escape, the Close button or clicking the backdrop closes it and returns keyboard focus to the gear. While open, keyboard focus stays within the overlay and its reachable gear, and the app behind it is inert; dismissal does not also activate the forest or close the arc drawer.

2.7 · The gear overlay has Projects, Settings, Updates and Help sections. The app owns the overlay frame, project switcher and existing Check for updates surface; the agent link mounts its existing per-user Settings panel; app-setup mounts its existing Help surface, including its first-run offer. Settings and updates retain their existing reader, writer and action behaviour. The section navigation has room to grow as settings are added.

2.8 · An always-visible full-width 48 px app bar holds a 36 px gear at the right and, at the left, the factory icon and Projects tabs (2.15). The left rail (2.39) and the forest beside it start directly below it, at 48 px, the forest and its controls never under the rail. With the overlay closed, the forest receives pointer input beside the rail and below the bar. The backdrop click that closes the overlay is consumed; subsequent forest input works. The existing data-state and data-drew smoke readings remain valid.
2.9 · A capture settles each requested animation frame before measuring or taking a picture
2.10 · A capture names a seed story's file by the package the seed's own story title gives, from a shared seed, so a later rename of the live package cannot desync it
2.11 · The empty page shows storytree's mark drawn in the page theme's own colours, light or dark, from no file
2.12 · A capture's stand-in bridge opens the page with the first-run guide already seen, so it pictures the globe; a capture of the guide itself opts back in to a first launch
2.13 · A capture whose browser close hangs after disconnect still ends
2.14 · A hung close kills the real browser's process and lets its pipes go

2.15 · The app bar holds two tabs: a factory icon that switches straight to the user's factory (greyed "No factory yet" without one), and "Projects", which always reads Projects and opens a dropdown of the products ending with "New project…"; after them a label names the product on show, with a button that copies its name
2.16 · A capture's stand-in bridge hides every teaching card as it appears, so none intercepts the capture's clicks; a capture of the cards themselves opts back in to seeing them
2.17 · The window mounts a switched-on stand-in surface's view from the factory
2.18 · An evidence capture's build goes to the checkout's ignored build folder, never beside the evidence it serves
2.19 · The capture kit's build holds every file its page names, the road worker's script included

2.20 · The desktop renderer writes every failure it catches to the console (so app.log), including those it does not show: a failed surfaces read (every surface on), a failed projects poll or forest read once drawn, and a failed start mark
2.21 · The capture kit's page runs React's production build, as the shipped app's does
2.22 · A desktop page opened with a problem says the library could not be opened, and why, and reads no projects
2.23 · A failed projects read shows its reason only while nothing is on show; a drawn forest or the empty page stays
2.24 · A failed project choice says why in place of the project and reads the projects again; a failed surfaces read mounts every surface
2.25 · A surface switched or set in the Surfaces menu draws the project on show again, as the settings now say
2.26 · A read or mount that lands after the user switched project changes nothing on show, and what it mounted is let go
2.27 · The forest kept at the last start is drawn at once, marked not fresh; a first read that fails says so over it, or over the page when none was kept, and once drawn a failure changes nothing
2.28 · A territory click opens its story on that capability, and a redraw of the open story keeps its open details, the panel tree's place and the popped-out tree
2.29 · Teaching cards hear whether the project on show is the factory, and each card is placed beside its target on the page
2.30 · Each start-timing mark is sent once, however often the page reaches it, and what the forest drew joins the page's census beside other surfaces' readings
2.31 · A capture launches the newest Chromium its browsers folder holds when Playwright's pinned one is missing
2.36 · A capture launch that finds no Chromium to take the pinned one's place fails naming CAPTURE_CHROMIUM and what the browsers folder holds
2.37 · A start with a kept forest is marked settled only once the globe has drawn a frame of what is on show after the fresh tree
2.38 · A capture on a live library answers the page with the app's own reads, its first activity read bounded to the newest lines and its changes folded

2.39 · The sessions list and the arcs each mount in their tab of one full-height left rail down the page's left, Sessions then Arcs, one tab on show at a time; a project opens on the tab it last showed, kept per project in the page's storage, and on Arcs with none kept; the Arcs tab badges what waits on the owner there, and none waiting shows no badge; a surface switched off has no tab, and with both off there is no rail
2.40 · The arcs read nothing until the page's start is settled, or until the forest's first read fails
2.41 · The arcs mount once the forest has asked its first tree read, at its first news or its first failed read, so their drawing never holds that read back

capabilities.title: 3 · Surfaces
capabilities.description: The app's window hosts the surfaces for the project on show: the forest, which the app opens on (until it lands, today's plain list), with the arc surface as an overlay that the forest hosts. The page cannot reach the database, so the app carries everything a surface reads to it, and tells the surfaces when the project changes.

contracts.title: 2.1 · Two separate processes write lines for two sessions, and reading from the start returns every line once, in the order written.
2.2 · Reading "since line N" returns only the lines after N, in order, each carrying the number to pass next time.
2.3 · Lines written for project "site" never appear when reading project "app".
2.4 · The log never shows up in the library's list of projects, and writing lines leaves the library's own records and change feed untouched.

2.5 · The log opens on whichever server the library resolved to, reached through the library's connection: lines two machines write for one project on one Cloud SQL instance are both read back from either, in order (live, opt-in).

2.6 · A line may name the earlier line of its own project's log that caused it (`causedBy`, ADR-0746 D2), and reads back naming it. A line naming a line its project's log does not hold (another project's, or none) is refused, whether appended alone or under the project's lock, and nothing is written.

2.7 · A bounded read sends only the lines it asks for, oldest first: by kind, session, cursor and time, by a field's value, values or absence, by a field carried, the latest for each key, the newest or oldest few, and inside folders whatever their case or slashes, with the fields it never reads left out.
2.8 · A read inside folders, latest line per session, on a log of many lines elsewhere is served by an index: it never scans the project's whole log

2.9 · An activity line can be formatted with its complete recorded command, including quotes and line breaks, for both started and finished commands; its number, time, session, kind and recorded cause remain visible. Compact formatting still clips long commands to 60 characters.

2.10 · A claim-refused line's text names the part, the session holding it, the file whose edit asked for it and the refused session's reason; a claimed line's text names its file and the session it was taken over from

2.11 · A line appended for a hook event is not added again when the log holds a line exactly like it, of the same event, that came the other way within two minutes of its time; the same way twice adds it twice

2.12 · A log opened in a storytree home whose settings name an experiment and arm stamps both on every line it writes (ADR-1064 D2); a log opened in a home that names none writes its lines without them.

2.13 · Lines written earlier, appended as one batch, go in at their own times and in order in a few round trips however many they are; a line exactly like one the log holds at that time, or like an earlier one of the batch, is added once, and a line of an event that came the other way within two minutes is kept once
3.1 · The page can ask the app for the library's changes and the agent log's new lines since a point, for the project on show, and only newer ones come back.
3.2 · A name that is not a project is refused, and never created.
3.3 · The smoke check, pointed at the surface on show, passes only if that surface says it drew every story and capability of the project.
3.4 · The page can ask the app for a story's or capability's shelf of front covers, and for the artifacts that link to an artifact, for the project on show.

3.5 · The page can ask the app for the context readings of named sessions in the project on show (agent link 9.5, 9.8), each parsed from the transcript records in the shared log, with no access to the machine the session ran on (ADR-0749 D3); a session with none named reads as an absence, and a name that is not a project is refused.

3.6 · The page can ask the app for a session's window in the project on show (agent link 9.10), or several sessions' in one ask that reads the log once, parsed from the transcript records in the shared log, with no access to the machine the session ran on (ADR-0749 D3); a session with none named reads as an absence.

3.7 · The Surfaces menu lists every surface with its switch and its settings; a surface switched off is saved to the settings file and reads back off, and one that follows it goes off with it; switching an always-on or unknown surface, or to an unknown choice, is refused with its reason and the file is untouched.

3.9 · After an app start, context readings and single or batched session windows take only the requested sessions’ latest transcript references from the activity log; the bytes read do not grow with the project’s activity history.

3.10 · After a restart the app reuses stored transcript records and fetches only appended records, preserving token counts, composition, historical openings, compactions and kept segments; retention keeps the final readings before raw records expire.
3.11 · The app reads the folders this machine imports for the project on show, so its survey draws the project's mapped stories; a name that is not a project is refused

3.12 · The desktop app's Surfaces menu lists the surfaces named by the manifests of the story packages it depends on, as the plugin loader composes them into its bundle and as its `#parts/surfaces` gives them run unbundled: the forest's, then the arc surface's
3.13 · The page can ask the app for the system notes the project on show reads from its factory
3.14 · The app reads where a project sits among factories, from its library already open, and whether it builds itself

2.16 · settings.json names the story parts switched off on this computer ("parts-off"): setPartOff switches one off or on and returns the parts off, sorted, leaving the other settings as they were; readPartsOff reads them alone, none when it names none; the core is refused with the reason and nothing written; a damaged value is reported naming the file
3.15 · Every canvas, gear menu tab and dialog the app opens carries a declared surface id, and the corner names it
3.16 · An agent switches the factory folder with the switch_factory tool, and settings show says who switched it
3.17 · The whole desktop page, every story's surface mounted in it, bundles for the browser as the app's build bundles it

capabilities.title: 4 · Updates
capabilities.description:
The app keeps itself up to date by itself: on the owner's machine it runs from its own copy of merged main, notices new merges within a few minutes, and rebuilds and restarts itself in the background, so it never runs unmerged work and nobody rebuilds it by hand. Check for updates in the top-right gear asks that same merged-main updater to check now and shows the running build and its progress or failure. A ready build waits with the window open until no seed or start-up or daily snapshot is being written. A checkout explains that it does not update itself. Installed apps select releases from their own channel: development follows each merged release; stable follows only the owner-pinned existing build (ADR-0871). As built (increment_aca4e6853237): an installed app's downloaded release waits for a quiet moment (packages/app whenToInstall: ten minutes after launch, ten minutes without window input or agent activity from a session that has not ended), because a first install was replaced 17 seconds after setup said the app was open (packages/app-setup/evidence/acceptance, F1). The gear answers from the release updater in an installed app, marks itself with a dot while an update is pending, and its Restart to update installs at once. A seed or snapshot still holds any restart, including one requested from the gear. The owner accepted contracts 4.4 and 4.7's wording for this on 2026-09-29 (question_df551985ad62).

As built (increment_c3e1441890f9, contract 4.12): installed release updates read named, independent run holds under the app home/update-holds before each automatic installation. packages/app/src/updates/hold-run.mjs wraps a foreground command, publishes its hold before launch, removes it on return and preserves its exit code. Holds expire after the requested positive duration, at most six hours; overlapping runs do not release one another. Downloads continue, the pending status names the run, and the user's Restart to update still overrides holds while respecting seed writes and snapshots. The standalone wrapper and usage/proof are in packages/app/evidence/update-hold. No laptop acceptance run is part of this implementation.


As built (increment_402e76453e34, contract 4.17): the follow-main updater start-checks each new build before it may restart into it (apps/desktop/src/main/start-check.ts, wrapping follow-main's build through mainUpdates' update option). The build is started with --start-check, which goes only as far as registering the main process's handlers and exits 0: no library, no network, so a library on Cloud SQL or a local Postgres the running app holds never holds back a good build. A check that does not exit 0 within 60 s fails the build as 4.2 does, and that commit is remembered and not rebuilt. Lifecycle 1.13: run()'s rejection now ends the app (exit 1) instead of leaving it half-started holding the single-instance lock.

As built (increment_78ac958384c9, contracts 4.4 and 4.13): the follow-main updater restarts into a built main commit only at the moment the user's install choice allows, as a downloaded release does. Owner, 2026-10-21: the follow-main app "keeps closing on me" (app.log held 1,135 restarts). mainUpdates takes a quiet option; the desktop builds one quietMoment check (packages/app/src/updates/install-moment.ts: whenToInstall over launch time, window use, agent activity and the saved install choice) and gives it to both updaters. A built commit waiting for that moment reads pending, so the gear offers Restart to update, which restarts at once in every mode; seeds and snapshots still hold either restart. Settings → Updates offers When updates install in an app following main as well, and a pending update says when it installs: at the next quiet moment, during quiet hours, or when you click Restart to update. With agents working on the laptop most of the day, quiet mode may rarely find a moment; quiet hours is the predictable choice.

contracts.title: 4.4 · An installed app checks for a newer published release offered by its own release channel, downloads and verifies it, and installs it only at a quiet moment: not in the first ten minutes after a launch, not while the window has been used or an agent session has worked in the last ten minutes, and never while a library seed or project snapshot is being written. The user can install it from the gear without waiting for a quiet moment, but seeds and snapshots still hold the restart with the window open and the update pending. Installing stops its database and restarts through the platform's installer into the new app using the app's lifecycle handoff.
4.5 · A failed release check or download leaves the app running and can be retried; equal and older releases never replace it, concurrent checks share one download, and quitting stops updates.

4.6 · Releases contain only work merged to main and verified on all three systems by main's own CI run of that commit; every later main build has a higher version, and a rerun cannot replace a newer published release. One platform's failure holds only that platform: a release publishes with every platform whose build is complete, and a platform whose build is not keeps its last good build's update feed and installer entry, so an installed app never meets a release that lacks its own platform's feed, and its one-liner installs the last build that has its platform. Every asset is uploaded into the draft before it publishes, and publishing is its last write: a late platform's build waits for the next version; nothing is uploaded to a published release.

4.7 · Check for updates in the gear checks the published releases now, using the same updater as the automatic check. Concurrent requests share the work. If no newer build is needed, the menu says the app is up to date and identifies the running build.

4.8 · The menu shows when a new build is ready or restarting. A ready build restarts the app through the existing lifecycle, waiting with the window open while a seed writes the library or a start-up or daily project snapshot is being written, including when the user asks from the menu; waiting neither downloads the ready build again nor starts a second restart.
4.9 · A failed manual update check or download shows its reason, leaves the running app alone, and can be retried from the gear.

4.10 · In a copy that does not install releases (a development checkout, a portable build), Check for updates explains that it does not update itself; the request neither fetches a build nor restarts the app.

4.12 · A named acceptance run can hold automatic release installation until it releases its hold or a finite ceiling expires; overlapping runs keep independent holds. Downloads continue, and an explicit Restart to update still installs once no seed or project snapshot is being written.

4.13 · The user chooses when a downloaded release may install itself: whenever quiet (the default), only inside their daily quiet hours, or never on its own (manual only); the quiet-moment rule still applies inside the hours, and their own Restart to update installs in every mode once no seed or project snapshot is being written.

4.14 · The gear's Updates section shows which install choice is on and, for quiet hours, when the next automatic install may happen; changing it there saves it, and a refused change shows its reason and keeps the old choice
4.15 · Stable installs use only the owner pin; alpha follows each release, with a durable channel that survives upgrades
4.16 · Pin an existing released build without rebuilding it, recording landed increment notes since the preceding pin and refusing a concurrent overwrite

4.17 · A release whose installed app cannot start never publishes: the release's install check starts the installed build's main process and fails unless it exits 0 in time with no promise rejection left unhandled
4.19 · An installed app's releases.log keeps the update lines a person reads and stays bounded

4.20 · The release signs the Mac build with the Developer ID in a job that installs nothing, and gives Apple's notarisation a bounded wait, when the signing secrets are present; stays ad-hoc when they are absent; and refuses a signed build Apple could not be asked to notarise

4.21 · An installed app knows it is installed (Windows by the installer's marker, a Mac by the delivery record naming its bundle, Linux by the delivery record naming the folder that holds its AppImage) and follows published releases on Windows, on Linux, or as a Developer ID signed Mac build
4.22 · A release rehearsal builds, signs and checks every platform's installers on a branch, and never drafts, uploads or publishes

4.23 · `storytree release candidate` names the newest published build fit to pin as stable: it covers every platform the pin covers, its release run published it with the Mac acceptance run passing, it has been out at least 24 hours, and no open friction or question names a regression in it or an earlier unpinned build; it prints that evidence and the notes a pin would publish, names what passed over each newer build, and changes nothing
4.24 · The user chooses the update channel, alpha or stable, in the gear; stable stays the default, and a switch takes effect on the updater's next check

4.25 · `storytree release pin` publishes a build as stable only once its fresh-install sweep passed: the stable routine's "Pin 0.3.N as stable?" question for that exact build, raised only after the old-laptop acceptance run passed it, unless retired; without it the pin refuses, publishes nothing and says how to run the sweep; the pin records the pass it stood on. A preview only reads, a move back to a build pinned before does not wait, and an expedited urgent fix waives the sweep as it waives the soak (ADR-1032 D7)
4.26 · After a repository cut-over, a stable pin's notes leave out work closed before it, whose number is the old repository's, and link work closed after it to the new repository
4.27 · A Windows update downloads only its changed blocks and verifies, even after an earlier downloaded update was never installed

4.28 · A release's packaged app cannot be run as plain Node, take NODE_OPTIONS or Node's inspector flags, or load its app from outside its own checked archive: each system's install check reads the built executable's fuses and fails unless each is set as the build sets them

4.29 · A failed read or change in the gear's Updates section is written to the console (so app.log) and shown: Update channel, When updates install and Open at sign-in show a failed first read, unchangeable, instead of vanishing, and a hidden switch or error line is never displayed
4.30 · A following app checks for a release at start and every three minutes until it quits; a failed check is logged and the next goes ahead, and a waiting release logs when it installs
4.31 · Only an installed Linux AppImage refreshes the agent tools beside it, and a refresh that fails is said
4.32 · The gear offers the update channel only where releases install themselves, and never in a smoke check
4.33 · The running app reports Electron's version when packaged, else its checkout's, else 0.3.0

capabilities.title: 5 · Recorder
capabilities.description: In the page: recognises each catalogue action its user takes from the input and the page's settled seam, and records its response, long frames up to settled (count and longest), settled time, whether progress was on show, its name and a size hint, handing them to the app in batches only when no action is under way.

contracts.title: 5.1 · A catalogue action its user takes becomes one reading of its response, long frames, settled time, progress, name and size
5.2 · Readings reach the app in batches, never between an action's input and its settling
5.3 · A drag that turns the map becomes one reading of its frames (p50, p95, longest and how many over 50 ms), named by the view it turned

capabilities.title: 6 · Readings file
capabilities.description: In the app's main process: appends each batch of readings, stamped with the app's version and time, to a bounded file in the app's home (STORYTREE_HOME), dropping the oldest past 30 days or 5 MB. Nothing is sent anywhere and nothing is written to the library.

contracts.title: 6.1 · Readings are kept in one file in the app's home, the oldest dropped past 30 days or 5 MB

capabilities.title: 7 · Lag report
capabilities.description: `storytree lag`: per action, over the last seven days, the count, median, 75th percentile and worst of the response, longest frame and settled time against the action's budget, the worst action first, saying so when an action has fewer than ten readings.

contracts.title: 7.1 · The report prints each action's count, median, 75th percentile and worst over seven days against its budget, worst first

capabilities.title: 1 · Story nodes
capabilities.description: The forest keeps one story node for every story in the project: where the story sits in the forest, with its title and its overall health. Nodes follow the library, so a new story appears as a new node and a retired story's node goes, with nothing arranged by hand.

contracts.title: 1.1 · Three stories give three story nodes, each with its title and its overall health as the agent reports it.
1.2 · Adding a story to the library adds a node, and retiring a story removes its node.

1.3 · A story's place is its row by dependency depth and its slot in the row: the bottom row has the story most depended on in the middle and the rest outward, a higher row is ordered by where its dependencies sit, and a loop in the dependencies never stops the layout (ADR-0839); the glass sheet lays each row out as a column of its own (1.12).
1.4 · A story's place is in a row above every story it depends on, and stories that depend on nothing share the bottom row (ADR-0839).
1.5 · Adding a dependency moves the dependent's island up a row (ADR-0839).

1.9 · A story's row is ranked by the stories its code's derived edges reach (with or without a capability at either end) together with its capabilities' recorded dependsOn rolled up to stories; package.json fields rank nothing; a project without a survey keeps the roll-up (ADR-0991 D2, D3).
1.10 · A five-story forest opens on the glass sheet with every nameplate readable, in a row and in a chain

1.11 · A mapped story sits in a row below the mapped stories whose code imports it, by the survey's roads among mapped islands, and a built story sits above the mapped story its package depends on; a loop among them still draws every island

1.12 · On the glass sheet a story's depth runs west to east: the foundation stories stand at the west edge, each deeper depth east of every shallower one, and stories of one depth spread north to south, clear of each other (ADR-1043 D2)

1.13 · The desktop's answer to the page's code survey answers a project whose origin has no fetchable main with no code rather than a rejection, so no handler stack is logged per poll; it says the refusal once in app.log per folder and reason, naming why, and says once when that folder's main can be surveyed again.

capabilities.title: 2 · Capability tree
capabilities.description: Each story node carries its capability tree: the story's capabilities, which ones build on which, and where each one stands, from planned through built to landed, and it grows as they land. Where a capability stands comes from two records kept side by side: the arc surface's rule for planned, in progress or landed, and the health the agent reports for its tests, always labelled as the agent's own.

contracts.title: 2.1 · A story with four capabilities, planned, being built, landed and reported passing, and landed with a failing report, gives a seedling, a seedling, a full green tree and a dead tree, in build order, each with the capabilities it builds on.
2.2 · A capability the agent reports red while it is being built stays a seedling.
2.3 · A landed capability with nothing reported is a pale tree.
2.4 · A story with no capabilities yet shows one seedling, so a new story is never invisible.

capabilities.title: 3 · Story node render
capabilities.description: The page opens in Forest mode, drawing every story node on the globe as a flat island cut into its capabilities' territories (ADR-0804 D1, D2) with the library core beneath them. Forest / Library switches this one globe (ADR-0660 D4): Library hides the story nodes and shows the knowledge points alone. You can turn and zoom in either mode, hover a visible artifact dot to see its title, and click a dot to read its summary in the right-hand story-panel slot (ADR-0661 D1/D2). Forest also lets you open a story by clicking its island. An artifact card and a story panel replace one another; Close and Escape dismiss the card. Switching modes preserves the scene, camera, rotation and zoom. Each launch defaults to Forest, with no saved mode. The flat forest and separate Look-inside view remain unavailable (ADR-0655).

contracts.title: 4.1 · Each island is a flat plate tangent to the big sphere at its spot (the glass sheet is its near pole), with its low ground above the sphere.
4.4 · Every recorded capability link between islands is one unbroken road across the glass, from dock to dock; a link within an island has none.
4.5 · An island on the globe is one ground surface with a coast line on each rim, lying on the globe's sphere, and marks laid on its land sit on that surface.
4.6 · A sideways CSS-pixel offset moves the glass sheet's perspective picture by that many pixels without moving or turning the eye.
4.7 · The map independently hides its island grounds and roads while keeping its camera and mounted plate children; hiding the whole exterior still preserves its inside.

4.8 · A lit link's lane is one unbroken strip from its capability's territory on the island built on, along its road between islands, to its capability's territory on the island building on it, following only lines drawn on each island; it is a thread of one width down the middle of its road, narrower than the narrowest road, with a soft glow in its colour that lanes sharing a stretch lay once between them, upstream blue and downstream violet, with a small mark in its colour at each end; where both colours share a road or an end, they remain distinguishable side by side

4.9 · Every lane of a selection starts at once and grows from its start by physical distance at one steady pace in its animation clock, so the selection settles in its longest lane's time; one warm head shows per shared stretch of one colour, slow frames preserve visible growth, and reduced motion shows every lane whole immediately with no head
4.10 · The globe draws nothing while its canvas is off screen, and draws again as soon as any of it is back
4.11 · An island facing the viewer hides whatever lies behind it, and nothing laid on its own land; an island seen from behind, through the glass, hides nothing

4.12 · A road between islands follows the globe's surface: no stretch of it cuts through the glass or rises above the islands' land, and it ends on its island's coast as drawn, however far round the globe its islands sit
4.13 · A capability link naming a capability on no island is left out on its own: every other road is still drawn, and the notice names what was left out
4.14 · A road to islands far round the globe is routed up to their coast: the chart it is routed on is centred on the islands, so none is stretched far past its coast and no road stops short of it
4.15 · When the browser hands the globe's drawing context back, the globe draws itself again, as it was

4.16 · Live roads grow by distance from dependency to dependent on first display and arrival; established shared roads stay drawn, unrelated updates preserve progress, and reduced motion shows the complete roads immediately

4.17 · Showing a hidden roads surface draws its pathways by distance from dependency to dependent over one second; rerenders preserve progress, recorded arrivals remain authoritative, and reduced motion shows the permitted roads immediately
4.19 · A road may end on an island as a whole, named by its story, as well as on a capability on it
4.21 · A layout draws its islands at once and its roads when routed, off the page's main thread where the page offers a road worker; an overtaken routing draws nothing
4.22 · On the glass sheet each island stands at the place on the sheet it is given and faces the eye square-on, within a degree, and the eye's depth range stays tight around the sheet
4.23 · On the glass sheet every island is a raised plate of one shared thickness, its sides running from its land down to the glass, so it reads as solid land standing on the glass (ADR-1059 D2)
4.24 · On the glass sheet a hollow island is its coast line alone, hiding nothing beneath it, and turns solid again (ADR-1061 D2)

4.25 · Under smoked glass (the Stories look) what hangs under the glass sheet shows by the angle: hidden from well above, at the top resting tilt, in view from near level and from below, drawn behind the glass from above and over it from below (ADR-1062 D4)

4.26 · The glass sheet is seen in perspective: nearer is drawn bigger, a zoom moves the eye toward the middle of the view and reads back as the zoom asked for, and the sheet stays between the near and far planes (ADR-1062 D1)
4.27 · The glass sheet is a lit slab: the glass has a visible thickness with a rim round both faces, and its edge and every island's sides are shaded by the scene's lights (ADR-1062 D1)

4.28 · Under clear glass (the Library look) what hangs beneath the glass sheet shows at every angle, from straight above to straight below, and the glass clears and smokes again without moving (ADR-1062 D3, D4)
4.29 · A plumbing call is drawn as a road between the two islands it joins, one per kind
4.30 · A plumbing road is not a dependency: it joins no capability link, widens no road and lights no lane
4.31 · Each plumbing road is labelled at its middle with its kind's words only, never a value word
4.32 · A plumbing road reads as a different kind of road from a dependency
4.33 · In a recorded growth a plumbing road shows once both its islands have risen, never before
4.34 · A layout's plumbing roads are routed and kept like its capability roads
4.35 · DOM laid over the sheet (a plumbing label, the roads notice) shows whenever the sheet opens, again included, and unmounts no React root while React renders
1.1 · With a cover A, links A → B → C and a shortcut A → C, C stays at depth 3: the shelf-to-cover step counts as 1. Visits and incoming-link counts never change that depth.

1.2 · An artifact reached by two shelves appears once, at its greatest depth, and names both entrances. A front cover keeps its own shelf as its home, and another shared artifact hangs under the oldest reachable shelf, with a stable tie-break.

1.3 · With A → B → C → B and C → D, B and C share a loop marked as an error at group depth 2, and D is at 3. An unreachable loop, like any unreachable artifact, is classified as no shelf, with no depth.
1.4 · Forty covers on their shelves and five artifacts on none, with no links, give forty artifacts at depth 1 and five with no shelf route, with no invented links. An empty shelf says it is empty.
1.5 · The globe draws every shelf-placed artifact once beneath its home island at its computed longest-chain depth. Ghosts, proposals and retired artifacts add no points.

1.6 · No-shelf artifacts fill a deterministic ball within 0.55 globe radii. Their centres remain at least 0.035 radii apart and at least that far from drawn shelf points, above the 0.012-radii dot diameter; every dot is wholly inside the shell. They gain no depth or invented shelf, and an empty corpus draws no points.

1.7 · Forest and Library submit the same complete set of eligible artifact points at the same positions and computed depths, with the same separated no-shelf artifacts; hiding story nodes leaves the live core mounted.
1.9 · Replaying a growth, each note appears beneath its home once the replay reaches its recorded date, in recorded order

1.10 · Under the glass sheet a note one island's links reach hangs beneath it, one step deeper per computed depth; a note no shelf reaches that links to hung knowledge hangs one step below the deepest note it links to; and each stored link between two drawn notes is one line (ADR-1043 D5, ADR-1063 D1, D2)
1.11 · Under the glass sheet no links show at rest; selecting a story shows exactly the links that touch its notes (ADR-1061 D3)

1.12 · Under the glass sheet a note whose links reach two or more islands settles between them, nearer the one it has more links to, and the many notes citing one note keep room from each other at their depth (ADR-1063 D1)
1.13 · The same library always hangs the same way under the glass sheet, and adding one note moves no other note by more than a third of a note's room (ADR-1063 D1)

1.14 · Under the glass sheet notes with no links, or linked only among themselves, lie on one floor below the deepest hanging note, spread evenly across the islands' footprint with each linked group kept together, drawn faintly; nothing lies in a pool along any edge (ADR-1063 D3)
1.15 · Selecting a story lights every note pulled toward its island under the glass sheet, including notes between it and another island; the rest are quieter (ADR-1063 D4)

dependsOn.title: 4 · Look inside and inspect an artifact

contracts.title: 4.1 · Clicking an artifact dot in Forest or Library opens the existing pinned-artifact card in the right-hand story-panel slot. It shows kind, title and description or another summary field; with no summary it shows the whole text. It contains no links list, read counts, depth or entrances.

4.6 · Opening an artifact card closes an open story panel, and opening a story closes the card. Close and Escape dismiss the card. The shared core pin and summary renderer serve both globe modes without writing to the library.

4.7 · With no session selected, no session lights a note, though the listed sessions have read them: the knowledge dots stay unlit, with no shared marks and no lines; selecting a session lights exactly what it read (ADR-0921).

4.8 · Drilling into a listed session colours its orchestrator in the session's own colour and each subagent in a distinct shade of that hue; an unknown agent stays pale, and a session with no row keeps the fixed palette (ADR-0738).
4.9 · The globe's knowledge dots light exactly as the core does: nothing with none selected, or the selected session alone in its agents' colours (ADR-0738 D5, ADR-0921).

4.10 · A selected session's reading path draws as curved lines: from each full read to the same known agent's next, in recorded order, pointing to the later read, bowed away from the globe's centre, in its agents' colours, only when it has no window to read, a subagent's first read stepping from the session's latest full read before it (where it was spawned); otherwise its window's traversal draws instead (4.16, ADR-0756). With none selected no path draws (ADR-0921). A peek or an unknown agent draws none, and a curve never claims a followed link (ADR-0740).

4.12 · A new step's line grows from its earlier read to its later one (one agent's new steps one after another, different agents at once), and opening the view grows nothing. With a session selected one replay walks all its agents' steps in recorded order, growing each line and lighting each note as it is reached, holds the finished picture, then clears and replays (ADR-0797). No looping glow is drawn (ADR-0921). Reduced motion neither grows nor replays; paths carry no arrowheads and no wisp model (ADR-0742).

4.15 · A note lit by a new read stays unlit until the growing line into it arrives (including a line queued behind that agent's earlier steps), then lights in its session's colour; a note already lit, or reached only by steps read before the view opened, is never held (ADR-0742 D2).

4.16 · Selecting a session reads its window from the host and draws it on the knowledge dots (ADR-0756): one line per step from each note it opened in full to the next, in reading order (files between do not break the chain; a note gone from the library is stepped over; a step taken twice draws once), in the session's colour, solid where a stored link joins the two notes either way round and dotted where none does, growing toward the later note when new and then showing direction with a faint fill that runs from the earlier note to the later. A note whose read is in the window now has a ring; one compacted out since is lighter, and its lines fade with it; one only glimpsed is tinted faint with no line. An answer for a session no longer selected is dropped, and with none selected no window is drawn or asked for.

4.20 · A selected session's file opens join its traversal where the land hands the core a place for them (ADR-0804 D5): each file whose path names a placed surveyed file (any path ending packages/<package>/src/…) is a stop on the code's surface, beside the notes it opened, in reading order; a step between two files is solid when one imports the other and dotted otherwise, a step between a file and a note dives into the core (or rises out of it), a compacted file's read fades with its steps, and a path that names no placed file is stepped over, never drawn. The map hands it no file places since ADR-1212, so there every file open is stepped over and the chain runs note to note. Opening a capability lights its territory; an arc, an increment or any other plan record is drawn nowhere and breaks nothing.

4.18 · With no session selected, the core asks the host for no session's window, whatever the running-sessions list holds; selecting one asks for that session's window alone, and never again while its last ask is out (ADR-0921).

4.21 · Each knowledge dot is sized by its note's reach: the distinct sessions that read it in the last 90 days, a whole read counting 1 and a peek 0.3, a session once at its strongest read. Its area grows linearly from a visible floor for a note no session read (or when no reads are recorded) to a ceiling for the most-read note on the globe. A note a selected session lights or holds in its window keeps its size: that read shows in colour, brightness and rings (ADR-0926).

capabilities.title: 4 · Drill-down
capabilities.description: Clicking a story node opens a panel that explains the story in plain words: its sentences, and its capability tree, each capability pointing at the ones it builds on, including any in other stories, named with their story. The tree has a space of its own inside the panel, where the user drags it around and zooms it; it opens zoomed out to fit the whole tree, as far as the least zoom allows, and an icon in that space's corner opens the same tree in a larger window over the forest, which opens fitted too. Each capability's card says proposed, healthy, unhealthy or untested on a strip coloured as 0.2 coloured those words, with the agent's report and storytree's as labelled marks (ADR-0743, ADR-0744). Clicking one of the story's own capabilities, in the panel's tree or in the larger window, shows it below the panel's tree: its sentences, its health as the agent reports it, and its contracts on request (ADR-0659).

contracts.title: 4.1 · A story whose third capability builds on the first two gives its sentences, its capabilities in build order each with its sentences and its health as the agent reports it, and a diagram with exactly two arrows.
4.2 · A capability that builds on a capability in another story shows an arrow to it, named with that story, and that capability's card says its word.
4.3 · A capability with no description says "no description yet" instead of leaving a blank.
4.4 · A contract the agent reported red, then green, shows "red, then green"; one reported only green says so.
4.5 · Storytree's own column shows beside the agent's report only where something wrote it.

4.6 · The panel shows the story's sentences and its diagram, and below the diagram only the capability selected: its word, its sentences, its health as the agent reports it, and its contracts folded until asked for. No front cover shows in it.
4.7 · When a story opens, the capability shown is the first in build order that is not healthy, or the first if all are; one clicked stays shown, and a choice outside the story falls back.

4.8 · Each of the story's capabilities is a card you can click, marked when selected and tinted by its word (a healthy card edged green, an unhealthy one red), never by the agent's report; another story's capability is in the tree but cannot be clicked.

4.9 · The capability tree is a graph of fixed-size cards: each capability sits above the ones it builds on, and another story's capability sits one row below the capability that builds on it, not in one row with every other outside capability.

4.10 · Each card, another story's too, has a strip across its top saying its word, proposed, healthy, unhealthy or untested (ADR-0744), coloured as 0.2 coloured it (proposed amber, healthy green, unhealthy red, untested grey), and the agent's report and storytree's as marks labelled "the agent reports" and "storytree saw", storytree's only where something wrote it. The work state (planned, in progress, landed) is not on the card.

4.11 · The capability tree has its own space inside the panel, moved by dragging and zooming, with no scroll bars and never out of reach. It, and the larger window, open with the whole tree fitted in the frame and centred, never above full size nor below the least zoom; the larger window's "Fit" puts that view back. An icon in the panel space's corner, labelled "Open in a larger window", opens the larger window.

4.12 · The capability selected, when it is not healthy, says why under its word and who moves it (the agent, or you), naming the contracts that carry it; a contract whose last verdict was not re-run says "last seen failing <date>, not re-run since"; a healthy one says nothing more.

4.13 · In a project whose health nothing verifies, a built capability's card and detail lead with what the agent reports, labelled as the agent's, and say storytree does not check this project's tests yet, never untested or who moves it
4.14 · A parked capability's card keeps its word and reason and says it is parked, naming the arc
4.15 · A mapped story's panel says it is mapped: here before storytree, assumed to be working, with its file and line counts, and shows no health

4.16 · Opening a story's island, the smallest, the largest or the library's, answers within 100 ms with no frame over 50 ms, and its panel is open within 1 s or shows progress; closing the panel likewise (verified by the Mint box's lag run)
4.36 · A selected story's panel shows a minimal risk bar: its rating out of ten, the users it could reach and its extra checks with what sets each off, no graph

4.37 · Wherever storytree's verified colour shows, on a capability's card and detail and on each contract, it says its source: verified locally, from CI, or locally and from CI; a reason not green names the source of the contracts carrying it; an entry with no source recorded says none

capabilities.title: 5 · Agent capability claims
capabilities.description: Shows on the world what each running session holds. Each capability claimed by a session the agent link lists (4.12), whether or not the running-sessions list shows its row (capability 7 shows only the sessions at work, ADR-1225), carries one flag in that session's colour, standing inside the capability's territory (ADR-0968, which replaced the inset border band of ADR-0923 D1 and the outline of ADR-0825 D3). Each session has its own stable colour, the same on its flags and on its row, never the proven green or the needs-you amber. The flag keeps its size on screen and becomes a dot on an island too small to carry a pennant; it drops in with one ring at its foot when the claim arrives, stands still while held, furls and greys when its holder goes quiet, and lifts away when the claim is released or lands, with no movement under reduced motion. On an island with no surveyed code the claimed capability's equal share is marked as a staked lot, a dashed white line inside its border; a capability with no code on an island that has code draws nothing. No band, outline, fill or coast tint is drawn for a claim, so a territory's fill stays health's. A flag carries no visible agent name, reason text or hooks warning. It follows the agent link's claims and sessions, so a holder whose hooks have reported goes quiet after the quiet time; a holder whose hooks have never reported is never quiet as idle. Subagents and supervised lanes folded under a parent flag in the parent's colour, a session with no row flags nothing, and an increment claim draws nothing on the world (ADR-0923 D2). A growth replay flags the capabilities its recorded sessions held as it reaches them (contract 5.7). Missing hooks are reported by the agent link's setup check (capability 8, contract 8.5). *History: the wisps of ADR-0736 were removed by ADR-0804 D9; ADR-0825 D3 outlined a claimed territory and tinted the coast; ADR-0923 dropped the coast tint; ADR-0968 (2026-10-10) made the mark a flag and added lots.*

contracts.title: 5.1 · Session A claims "email form", and a flag in A's colour stands on that capability's territory, with no visible agent name or reason text; A's claim on a capability on a second island is flagged there too. An increment claim flags nothing, whatever its touches name (ADR-0968 D1, ADR-0923 D2).
5.2 · For a holder whose hooks have reported, after the quiet time with no new line its flags furl and grey; when A reports the capability landed, its flag lifts away.
5.3 · A session seen only through its tool calls keeps its flags unfurled even past the quiet time; the map draws no hooks warning.
5.4 · None of this changes how a capability's state is drawn.

5.5 · A session's colour is the same on every read, on its flags and on its row in the sessions list, and is never the proven-green colour. A subagent folded under its parent flags its claims in its parent's colour. A session the agent link no longer lists (4.12: ended, gone, or quiet past the leave-after) flags nothing; an idle one it still lists flags its claims, furled (5.2), though the sessions list shows no row for it (7.10, ADR-1225).
