capabilities.title: 1 · Manifests
capabilities.description: Reads the `storytree` manifests of the story packages a host depends on and returns the parts of one kind, in order, refusing a manifest that names what its package does not export.

contracts.title: 1.1 · storyParts(host, kind) returns the parts of that kind named by the `storytree` manifests of the packages the host's package.json depends on, each as { package, module, export }; a package with no manifest, or none for that kind, adds nothing
1.2 · A manifest part whose `from` is not a subpath its package exports, or that lacks an export name, is refused, naming the package and the part, and nothing is returned
1.3 · storyParts orders parts by their manifest's order, lowest first and unordered last, ties by package name then position in the manifest, whatever order the host lists its dependencies in

1.4 · storyServices(host) returns each service the manifests of the host's story packages declare, as { package, name, run, module, export }; one with no name, a run but "always" or { every: "<n>m" }, or an unexported from is refused, naming the package

capabilities.title: 2 · Build-time composition
capabilities.description: The writer of the parts list a build reads (question_efc2a06dacad, option A): a step, run as a command (`parts-list.ts <host> <file>`), that writes as data, for each `#parts/<kind>` the host's package.json imports, the parts the manifests of its dependencies name (in storyParts' order, each with the part it came from), the host's parts graph, and a fingerprint of every package.json it read. The builds that pack a bundled host run the step and read its list with a small resolver of their own, importing none of the loader's code, so a bundled host mounts its parts with no story named in its code. Unbundled, the same import is answered by capability 3.

contracts.title: 2.1 · The parts-list step writes, for each #parts/<kind> the host's package.json imports, every part its dependencies' manifests name in storyParts' order with the part each came from, an empty list for a kind no manifest names, the host's parts graph, and a fingerprint of each package.json it read

capabilities.title: 3 · Run-time composition
capabilities.description: A host run unbundled (under tsx, in tests and `pnpm storytree`) imports `#parts/<kind>` through its package.json's `imports`, which names a module of its own that composes the same parts at run time: storyParts, then each part's module imported as the host resolves it. The same import is answered at build time by capability 2, so a host's source is one form either way.

contracts.title: 3.1 · An unbundled host importing #parts/<kind>, which its package.json's imports maps to its own module calling composeParts, gets as its declarations every part's declarations concatenated in storyParts' order, and an empty list for a kind no manifest names

capabilities.title: 4 · Switching a part off
capabilities.description: Every list the loader composes knows which story part each declaration came from and what that part stands on, so a host can leave out the parts this computer's setting switches off and say so when one is asked for (ADR-1092 D2, D3).

contracts.title: 4.1 · A composed list carries, beside its declarations, the part each came from (its package name without the scope) and the host's parts graph: each package with a manifest the host depends on or reaches through one of them, and the parts its package.json depends on

4.2 · mount(composition, off) gives a host every declaration but those of a part `off` names and of every part standing on one however deep, and each part left out with the named part it is off because of; the core (library, plugin-loader, project-and-caller) and names the host lacks are ignored
4.3 · `settings set part <part> off` or `plugin <plugin>` names the command families, commands and tools the parts it switches off take away, and those the plugin adds in their place

4.4 · A host's parts graph also names each part another part takes only as a development dependency whose manifest declares services, with no edge from the one taking it, so switching it off leaves that one on

capabilities.title: 5 · Factory plugins
capabilities.description: A plugin in the user's factory folder, a package with a storytree manifest, stands in for a part of storytree this computer switches off: the loader reads the plugin's manifest from the folder the user chose (choosing it is the one-time approval, question_5867f490cdd6), loads the modules it names as ready-to-run JavaScript while the host starts, and the host mounts the plugin's declarations where the switched-off part's were. Switching the part back on mounts the built-in part again and the plugin not at all. A plugin is handed storytree's interface, never its insides (ADR-1112 D2): it exports declarations whose work is given its context by the host.

contracts.title: 5.1 · A factory plugin named to stand in for a part is loaded from this computer's factory folder (plugins/<plugin>/package.json, a storytree manifest naming ready-to-run modules) and mounted where the part's declarations were while that part is switched off, and not at all once it is on; a kind it does not name adds nothing
5.2 · A stand-in that cannot be loaded (no factory folder, no such plugin, no manifest, an unexported module, no list) leaves its part off, said with why, and the host still mounts the rest

5.3 · A factory plugin's manifest names the version of storytree's plugin interface it was written for: one this host honours is mounted, and one naming another version, or none, is left unmounted with its part off, said with the version it named and the one this host honours
5.4 · A plugin's exported file is found by its export name, and nothing else of the factory is

5.5 · `plugin new <plugin>` (the new_plugin tool) starts a plugin in this computer's factory folder that this storytree loads: standing in for a part, its family mounts and its verb answers, and its own test command passes its numbered test; a name taken, or one that is not one folder's, is refused, writing nothing

5.6 · `plugin check <plugin>` (the check_plugin tool) says whether this storytree would load a plugin in a part's place, and why not, switching nothing: a manifest of another shape, a module exporting no list, a family or verb missing what a door mounts are each said; one that loads is named with what it adds

5.7 · `plugin contract` (the plugin_contract tool) says what a factory plugin must contain: the plugin interface version this storytree honours, each kind a part can be stood in with and the hosts that mount it, a verb's shape and the answer its act returns

5.8 · A mounted factory plugin declares its own kinds of record in its manifest's recordKinds, named <plugin>.<kind>; with its part on it declares none, and a kind it cannot declare is left out with why.

5.9 · `plugin remove-records <plugin>` (the remove_plugin_records tool) lists a switched-off plugin's records before removing exactly those with --yes; it refuses a plugin switched on, and switching off removes nothing

5.10 · A plugin's manifest names its librarian's own database role and update right; storytree fences that role from it to the plugin's kinds, and the database refuses the librarian's write to a core kind
5.11 · plugin fence applies each mounted plugin's writers and librarian to the project's library, saying what each role was granted; plugin check names the librarian's role
5.12 · A plugin's manifest declares its long-running services, and plugin check loads them or says why not

5.13 · A factory plugin that stands in for no part is added under its own name: `plugin new <plugin>` with no --for, and `plugin check`, name `settings set part <plugin> plugin <plugin>`, and every host mounts it, after its own parts, while the setting names it, and not once it no longer does

5.14 · A plugin's manifest names its plan file inside its folder: `plugin check` counts its capabilities, and `plugin import-plan` writes it into the project's plan, adopting a story the first time, saying what it added, edited, retired and kept; a plan outside the plugin's folder, or not JSON, is refused saying why

5.15 · `plugin check` on a plugin made `--for <part>` (or given --for, or set to stand in for it) lists what that part provides that the plugin does not: its commands and tools, as the host's door composes them

5.16 · A plugin's manifest declares gate steps, each { name, when?, command }, which the base dev loop's gate runs: plugin check loads one declaring only gateSteps, saying how many, and refuses a step with no name or no command with why; plugin contract describes a gate step

5.17 · A plugin's manifest declares guidance, sections of the habits card: plugin check loads one declaring only guidance, saying how many, and refuses a section that is not text with why; plugin contract describes a section

5.18 · `plugin import-plan <plugin> --from <folder>` reads the plugin's plan from that factory folder instead of this computer's, so a lane imports from its own factory worktree right after its push; a folder that is not there is refused saying so

5.19 · A factory plugin named as the part it stands in for mounts alone in that part's place while the part is off, and the part alone once it is on, on every host (the command line, the gate, the window, the service host); what each provides is said as its own, and plugin check names `settings set part <part> plugin <part>` as switching that part off with it in its place
5.20 · A plugin's manifest declares arm checks and run holds: plugin check loads one declaring them, saying how many of each, and plugin contract describes each with the hosts that mount it

5.21 · The factory plugin this computer's setting does not name that declares a family is found by the family's name, with the part settings set part names it as (its manifest's for, else its own name); a named plugin, one that cannot be loaded, or no factory folder finds none.
5.22 · every factory plugin no stand-in names is listed with the part it would stand in for

capabilities.title: 1 · Project routing
capabilities.description: The first time an agent session starts in a folder that isn't a storytree project, storytree asks the user (through the agent) whether to set one up; if they say yes, this leaves a small marker in the folder naming the project, and from then on it routes everything an agent does anywhere in that folder to that project, whichever project the user happens to be looking at in the app. It never picks a project by itself: a folder the user hasn't said yes to is ignored, and when storytree isn't running it says so at once, so everything built on it quietly does nothing.

contracts.title: 1.1 · A folder whose marker names "site" gives "site" asked from the folder, from a sub-folder of it, and from a git worktree of it.
1.2 · A folder with no marker, in it or above it, gives "not a storytree project".
1.4 · With the app's database stopped, asking where to send activity answers "storytree isn't running" in well under a second.
1.5 · A leftover address from a crashed app counts as not running: it answers in well under a second and never hangs.

1.6 · With the library set to Cloud SQL, a project folder routes to that instance (its connection name and user) whether or not the app's local database is running, and no local address is tried; with it local, routing is exactly as in 1.1 to 1.5.

1.7 · Routing reads only the library setting: damage elsewhere in settings.json (an unusable context guidance, say) does not stop it, while a damaged library setting, or a file that is not a JSON object, refuses naming the file and is never read as local nor rewritten.

1.12 · A marker alone reaches no project (ADR-0942): a checkout whose marker names an existing project, with or without its identity, is refused until its trunk on this machine is approved, and a trunk recorded before approval counts as unapproved until it joins on purpose; an approved trunk and its git worktrees reach it.

1.15 · Project and caller's routing entry alone (@storytree/project-and-caller/routing) routes a folder: one that is no project gives "not a storytree project", and a project whose app is stopped gives "storytree isn't running", without the caller loading the package's root

1.16 · An authenticated local installation routes only through its private, matching versioned credential handoff; damaged or exposed material refuses without a passwordless fallback, while legacy discovery, app liveness and explicit remote routing remain usable
1.17 · Only a git worktree its trunk's repository registered inherits the trunk's project and approval; a copied or forged .git file pointing at a trunk makes no worktree of it

1.18 · A forgotten trunk's remembered approval opens nothing: removing the project from this machine, or deleting it everywhere, drops this machine's remembered approval for it, so its folder is refused until approved again (ADR-0942)

1.19 · An imported folder is recorded on its project beside the trunk, per machine, approved by the import; recording it again updates its repository and commit, and forgetting the trunk forgets its imports
1.20 · The projects with a trunk are read as one set across every machine: a forgotten trunk leaves it, and an imported folder is no trunk

1.21 · A folder's marker is .storytree/project.json, and a root .storytree.json is still read while projects move: the nearest marker at or above a folder names its project, and a folder holding both is routed by .storytree/project.json

capabilities.title: 2 · Settings
capabilities.description: The user's own settings on this computer, for every story: read and written by Project and caller's package (moved out of Session management by ADR-1025), set from the command line and from the app's settings panel (ADR-0728 D2, D3; ADR-0729; ADR-0739; ADR-0649). Per user only: one file, `settings.json`, in the storytree home (`STORYTREE_HOME`, else `~/.storytree/0.3`, capability 1) beside `project-choice.json`. Each setting has a name, a type, a default and a plain-language meaning. An unset setting reads as its default, marked as the default. A value of the wrong type, or a name that is not a setting, is refused with its reason and nothing is written. A settings file that cannot be read or is not valid is reported, naming the file and the problem; it is never silently replaced, and a set refuses to overwrite it.

contracts.title: 2.1 · In a throwaway storytree home with no settings file, `context-guidance` reads 600,000, marked as the default, with its type (tokens) and its meaning.

2.2 · `storytree settings set context-guidance 400000` writes it to `settings.json` in the storytree home, and `storytree settings show`, and a fresh read by Project and caller's reader, give 400,000 marked as set.
2.3 · Setting a name that is not a setting, or `context-guidance` to a value that is not a positive whole number, is refused naming why, and the settings file is left as it was.

2.4 · A settings file that is not valid JSON, or holds `context-guidance` of the wrong type, is reported on read naming the file and the problem, never read as the default; a set refuses to overwrite it, and the file is left byte for byte.

2.5 · With no library setting, `storytree settings show` reads the library location as `local`, marked default; `storytree settings set library cloudsql <instance> <user>` saves the Cloud SQL instance's connection name and the Google account to sign in as, and reads back as set; `storytree settings set library local` returns to local.

2.6 · `settings set library` with anything but `local`, or `cloudsql` with an instance not written project:region:instance or a user that is not an email, is refused with the reason, and the settings file is left byte for byte.

2.7 · Settings in the app’s gear opens a panel headed Settings, with “Yours on this computer · all projects”. Every setting returned by the reader has its current value, meaning, and default or set-by-you source; values can be saved with capability 2’s writers. A newly listed numeric setting needs no panel change.

2.8 · A refused value shows the writer’s exact reason beside its row, leaves the settings file byte for byte, retains the saved source, and can be corrected and retried. A successful save reads back when the panel reopens. Library location uses the same local/Cloud SQL writer and reports that changes apply when the app next opens.

2.9 · A failed read of the Settings panel shows the failure's reason and Retry, never fabricated defaults in place of the rows, and Retry reads again; a save whose transport fails shows its reason and leaves Save available for retry. The overlay that holds the panel (its focus loop with the reachable gear, Close or Escape returning focus to the gear, and its fit at narrow window sizes) is the app frame's: The app 2.6 and 2.7.

2.10 · With no settings file, `idle-after` reads 30 minutes, marked as the default; `storytree settings set idle-after 10m` sets it, and a value that is not a duration (such as `soon`, `0m` or `-5m`) is refused with its reason, and the settings file is left byte for byte. What the setting does to claims and sessions is Session management's Claims 5.43.

2.11 · With no settings file, `leave-after` reads 1 hour, marked as the default; `storytree settings set leave-after 2h` sets it, and a value that is not a duration is refused with its reason and the settings file left byte for byte (ADR-0754 D4; default from ADR-0758 D5).
2.14 · The app shows who decides what, read-only, from the habits card's own lines

capabilities.title: 5 · Portable user identity
capabilities.description: A trusted sign-in resolves to a durable Storytree user id. The identity-owned Cloud SQL users store retains linked provider+subject identities, the verified email and a replaceable WorkOS user pointer. Proof uses real PostgreSQL persistence to resolve first, repeat, linked and conflicting sign-ins without using email equality as identity.

contracts.title: 5.1 · A first trusted social sign-in persists a Storytree-owned user id, its verified email, the replaceable WorkOS user id and every linked Google, GitHub or Microsoft provider+subject identity; reopening the store returns that same user.

5.2 · A returning provider+subject identity resolves to its existing Storytree user id even if its email or WorkOS pointer changes; an unrelated provider+subject with the same email creates a different user.
5.3 · Authoritative linked identities join the existing user's identity set atomically; an identity set spanning two existing Storytree users is refused without changing either user.
5.4 · Concurrent resolutions of the same provider+subject create one Storytree user and return its same durable id.

5.5 · The server resolves a user only from a valid WorkOS session token and authoritative supported social identity evidence; invalid, expired or wrongly issued tokens, unverified email, unsupported providers or missing subjects are refused before any user is written.

capabilities.title: 6 · Social sign-in and session
capabilities.description: The desktop and storytree sign-in use the system browser to authenticate through WorkOS with Google, GitHub or Microsoft only. The identity package owns PKCE/device-flow orchestration, trusted session verification, session persistence, status and sign-out; clients contain no WorkOS API key. Proof covers successful and refused exchanges plus a real authorized staging journey; production activation remains an explicit owner prerequisite.

contracts.title: 6.1 · Desktop sign-in opens the system browser with PKCE, offers only Google, GitHub and Microsoft, and completes only its matching authorization response; cancellation or a mismatched response leaves the user signed out.

6.2 · storytree sign-in shows the verification URL and user code, waits according to the device-flow interval, and reports the signed-in Storytree user only after authorization; denied or expired authorization leaves it signed out.

6.3 · A restarted desktop restores its protected signed-in session, refuses unavailable secure storage instead of saving plaintext tokens, and sign-out removes its session so the next status is signed out.
6.4 · A signed-in CLI reports its Storytree user without revealing tokens, and sign-out removes its saved session so the next status is signed out.

6.5 · The desktop signs in only with a public WorkOS client ID configured, verifies WorkOS's access token itself against the client's published keys with no identity server, waits for the storytree-auth callback, and refuses a provider refusal, a failed exchange, a sign-out or a sign-in that never returns.

3.1 · Saving a `story` with no `title` is refused, the error names `title`, and nothing is written.
3.2 · An unknown field (for example `titel`) is refused and named.
3.3 · An unknown type is refused.
3.4 · Every stored record carries its schema version (1 today).

3.5 · Reading a record stamped with a version newer than this code knows is refused, never guessed at. The error names the record and both schema versions, gives the update and agent-link restart steps, and reports the running code commit distance behind locally fetched origin/main when known; unavailable Git information never masks the refusal or invents a distance.
3.6 · An `edit` that would leave the record invalid (for example blanking a required field) is refused, and nothing is written.
3.7 · A record written on an OLDER version of its type is read (`get`, `list`) upgraded to the current version, its upgrade steps applied in order. Reading it writes nothing.

3.8 · An `edit` of such a record merges onto its upgraded fields and stores it on the current version, in place, in the same all-or-nothing write. If the upgraded result does not fit, nothing is written.
3.9 · An older record that no upgrade step brings to the next version is refused by `get`, `list` and `edit`, with an error naming the missing step. It is never guessed at.

3.10 · A friction report written before reports carried a state reads with one worked out from its route and stamp (no route open, nothing dismissed, a stamp resolved, any other route routed), and its next write stores it so
3.11 · A story and a capability carry their prose as `text`, read back whole and in order; one written without it reads as before

3.12 · A process's schedule, time zone and precheck are validated: words the parser cannot read, a grace on any but a daily schedule, an unknown time zone, a precheck not on the fixed list, or a time zone or precheck on a process with no schedule are refused and named

3.13 · A process's schedule reads back as written, and as its rule (a daily schedule's grace in minutes), its times in its own time zone or the owner's, and its precheck as written; a process with no schedule reads as before

3.14 · A story carries a risk reading (a blast depth 1 to 3 and a blast radius 1 to 4 with its downstream stories, audience and users, each with the day read and why), and a story or capability its own guardrails (a check and whether a change or a release triggers it); a value out of range is refused and named, and a record written without them reads as before
3.15 · A kind a plugin declares, `<plugin>.<kind>` with its fields' shape as JSON Schema, is written and read back like a core kind, and read upgraded by the steps it declares as data.
3.16 · A dotted kind no loaded plugin declares is refused on write, and nothing is written.
3.17 · A write that breaks the shape its plugin declared is refused, naming each field at fault, and nothing is written.
3.18 · A plugin kind no loaded plugin declares reads dormant: kept intact and readable by id, hidden from lists, refused an edit; declared again, its records read as before.
3.19 · A write to a principle, guardrail, pattern, process, agent role or decision carries the mark of the outside text its writer had read; a write of any other kind carries none

capabilities.title: 3 · Arm repositories
capabilities.description: A public throwaway repository per arm in the storytree-ai organisation (ADR-1064 D3, as the owner amended it 2026-10-16), seeded from the task, with Linux-only CI, the merge queue on, and the task's verifier as a job; archived when the experiment ends. The task's hidden tests are never committed: CI fetches them at run time with a secret the lanes do not hold. Creating these repositories is approved by the owner's answer on question_b8a73d781784.

contracts.title: 3.1 · An arm's CI runs on Linux only: its own checks gate every pull request and merge-queue entry, and the task's hidden tests run only on each merge to main, fetched with a secret, out of the reach of the arm's code, reporting counts alone
3.2 · Making an arm's repository creates it public in storytree-ai, seeded from the starting tree with the arm's CI, sets its secrets through stdin, and turns the merge queue on for main
3.3 · Ending an experiment archives each of its arms' repositories

3.4 · An arm's workflow, which runs the hidden tests with their token after each merge, changes only with a code owner's review, and its one code owner is the identity its lanes act as, so no lane can approve its own change

capabilities.description: The experiment record, a new library kind (ADR-1064 D5): arms, hypotheses, measures, what counts as the variable helping, not helping or inconclusive, budget and stop rules. contracts.title: 4.1 · Freezing an experiment stamps the time once, and a run reads only a frozen one

capabilities.title: 5 · Per-merge points and curves
capabilities.description: One point per merge and the curves they make (ADR-1064 D4): each merge on an arm's repository writes an experiment_points row (experiment, arm, merge number, pull request, time, verifier passed and total, tokens to date, collisions to date, file growth, imports crossing capability lines, rework), and `storytree experiment curves <experiment> [--json]` prints them as a series per arm. Per-lane measures are read from labelled activity lines, the QA ledger and transcript records.

contracts.title: 5.1 · Recording an arm writes one point per merge to main, in merge order, with its hidden-tests counts and the tree's files and bytes, never twice, stopping at a merge whose run has not finished
5.2 · A merge whose arm workflow differs from the one it was seeded with is recorded as changed, and its curve flags it
5.3 · experiment curves prints each arm's points as a series, and --json gives them as data per arm
5.4 · Each point carries the tokens the arm's sessions had spent by its merge, read from the arm's own project's stored transcripts, and the curves give them
5.5 · Each point carries the arm's collisions by its merge: claims refused, pull requests gone red and, of those, conflicts with main, from the arm's own project's lines
5.6 · Each point carries its rework: the lines its merge removed that one of the five merges before it added, matched by file and text, a blank line or an older merge's never counted
5.7 · each point carries the imports crossing capability lines in the arm's tree at its merge, and the source lines they are counted over
5.8 · The seed the import pushed is point zero, with the counts its push's hidden-tests run printed against the untouched start, recorded once and before any merge, and the curves show it as the seed
5.9 · An arm recorded without the CI it was seeded with judges each merge's workflow against the one at its seed commit, still after the seed is recorded, and refuses when it has no seed to judge by
5.10 · Recording an experiment records each of its arms in turn, an arm that fails said without stopping the others, and says per arm what it wrote and where it waits
5.11 · Curves read a run's points by its record's id or its short name
5.12 · An arm whose tree keeps its code outside its stories’ packages still counts its source lines at each merge, and its crossings are unmeasured, never zero

capabilities.title: 4 · A watcher lands a handed-over pull request
capabilities.description: A session on any machine ends once its pull request is open and its gate is green, and hands the PR to a watcher with no model (packages/dev-loop/src/lanes/watch.mjs): `watch.mjs handover <pr> <increment>` runs `hand` on the box directly, or over `ssh mint` from another machine with the session's own id, refusing with the reason when the box is out of reach (ADR-0974). `hand` records the hand-off in ~/storytree-lanes/watch/, sets an event wait on the increment so no other session takes it while it lands, and starts the watcher if none runs. The watcher polls GitHub: on MERGED it clears the wait, closes the increment landed with the PR and releases the session's remaining claims; on a red (a failed check, a conflict with main, or an ejection from the merge queue) it clears the wait and starts one fix session for that PR, which fixes, pushes and hands back; after its fix limit it writes an owner wait with the PR and the logs. A conflict with main reads as one whatever else failed (13.18), gets one more fix session (13.12), and past that never waits on the owner: the hand-off is dropped and the increment goes back on its arc as ready work, its body naming the PR and its branch (13.20). A fix session whose branch moved while it ran is not counted when the next red is a conflict, and a cap on all sessions per PR (WATCH_FIX_CAP, 6) stops a loop (13.19). A fix session refused by another session's claim hands back with --refused and counts for nothing (13.14), and conflicts with main are merged by one fix session at a time, lowest pull request first (13.15). The watcher also owns a stopped release (ADR-1032 D2): every five minutes its look loop reads the latest published release, the release runs and main's CI runs from GitHub; a release attempt or main's newest CI run that failed is rerun once (main's, and a handed-over pull request's red, again up to a run's fourth attempt while every failed job is the runner's: no runner took it, or the browser crashed at launch, 4.29), and a stop that outlasts the rerun (main still red, the last two release attempts failed, or a commit green on main for over two hours in no published release) starts one fix session at a time, none while one lives or its pull request or question is open, and past the fix limit asks the owner on the release arc (arc_312aa103bfca) (13.16, 13.17). The watcher (`run`) is a keeper over its look loop (`watch`), which exits with the restart code once the dev loop's code in the shared checkout changes, so the keeper starts it again on the new code; `status` says when the running look loop's code differs from the checkout's, or predates the version it records (13.21). It is not an engine, so it counts against no engine slot; its fix sessions are. Founded on decision_e101df427118 (ADR-0955 D3). Every hour the look loop also reads main's first-parent history of the owner's secret-check exemptions list (.github/secret-check-exemptions.txt) from git and records one FYI per commit that changed the paths it exempts: what it added and took away, the pull request and who opened it; each FYI is about `<list>@<sha>`, which the library is asked for first, so a change is told once and none is missed between looks (4.42, increment_67dc251f5856: awareness, not prevention, question_82ab3da6eb69). The watcher and the sessions it starts run in freeOf's environment, without the handing-over session's id or its lane's run marker, so the lane runner does not stop them when that lane ends (4.43).

capabilities.title: 1 · Key store and resolver
capabilities.description: Keeps the keys storytree must hold in one auth.json in storytree's home, only the user can read and write it, and many processes can write it at once safely. It resolves a named key the same way in every process: an explicit value, then the file entry (a literal, or a `!<command>` run once per process), then the environment variable. `storytree auth set|list|remove` is its command-line front door: the cli family parses, calls this package and prints.

contracts.title: 1.1 · Saving a key creates `auth.json` in storytree's home (`STORYTREE_HOME` when set, else `~/.storytree/0.3`, the folder `settings.json` uses), readable and writable by the user alone: on macOS and Linux the file's mode is 0600; on Windows it relies on the user-profile folder's own permissions, and nothing changes them.

1.2 · Two writers saving different keys at once both survive: reading `auth.json` back after they finish finds both entries, because every write holds a file lock and writes a temporary file that is then renamed over `auth.json`, so a reader never sees a half-written file.

1.3 · Resolving a key returns, first to last, an explicit value given by the caller, then its `auth.json` entry, then its environment variable: with all three present the explicit value wins; with no explicit value a saved entry wins over the environment variable; with neither, the environment variable is returned; with none, resolving says the key is not set.

1.4 · An `auth.json` entry `!<command>` resolves to the command's standard output, trimmed, and resolving it again in the same process does not run the command again; a command that fails is an error naming the key and that its command failed, which never contains the command's output.

1.5 · `storytree auth set <name>` reads the value from standard input, takes none as an argument and never prints it; `storytree auth list` prints each key's name and where it resolves from (file, command or environment) and never a value; `storytree auth remove <name>` deletes that entry from `auth.json`, leaving the others.

capabilities.title: 1 · Postgres binaries
capabilities.description: Finds initdb, pg_ctl and postgres for this machine: from the @embedded-postgres package built for it (the x64 one on Windows arm64, run under emulation), or from the directory a packaged app ships them in.

contracts.title: 1.1 · The binaries come from this machine's @embedded-postgres package, and on Windows arm64 from the x64 one; with none installed, the error names every package it looked for.
1.2 · A directory handed over by a packaged app is used when it holds initdb, pg_ctl and postgres, and refused, naming it, when it does not.

capabilities.title: 2 · A server on a data directory
capabilities.description: Makes a cluster in a data directory the first time, asking every connection for the installation's password (SCRAM; a legacy trust cluster is converted at start), starts a server on it listening on 127.0.0.1 only, makes sure clients' ordinary role (storytree: may create databases, owns every database, no superuser) exists and owns what the superuser made before, hands back its url signing in as that role, and publishes the private connection handoff (ADR-0941) while it runs; stops it; while it runs, an owner record beside the directory (`<dataDir>.owner.json`) names the process that holds it, which is how others learn whether storytree is running and where.

contracts.title: 2.1 · A cluster is made only where there is none, asking every connection for the installation's password and listening on 127.0.0.1 only; a directory holding anything else is refused and left untouched.
2.2 · A started server answers SELECT 1 at the url handed back; stop stops it, a second stop is harmless, and it can be started again, on a port asked for.
2.3 · A start on a data directory a live process holds is refused with a DataDirInUseError naming that process and its owner, and the holder's server is left running.
2.4 · A server left running by a process that died is stopped and replaced, and a dead owner's record alone is cleared, so the start goes ahead.

2.5 · A start can carry server settings for that run, as the throwaway test server runs with fsync, synchronous commit and full-page writes off; a start without them keeps the cluster's own, and a setting that is not one plain word is refused before anything starts.
2.6 · The server lets in only a client with the installation's password, which it hands over privately while it runs
2.7 · A cluster made when local connections were trusted is given the password before its server starts again, keeping its data, and an interrupted start never reopens it
2.8 · Clients sign in as an ordinary role that owns storytree's databases, never as the superuser
2.9 · A throwaway test server can hand back the superuser's url beside its client's, for tests' setup, while its clients and handoff stay the ordinary role

2.10 · On Windows the sign-in is kept private beside a data directory whose folder lets this user change files but not take ownership (a checkout under C:\code): the access list is set without asking to change an owner the user already is
2.11 · On Windows a sign-in folder a failed first run left behind is made private before any sign-in goes into it

2.14 · Run as root (a cloud container), the Postgres tools and the server run as the unprivileged account nobody, which is handed the cluster, the server log and initdb's password file and let through the folders above them; run as anyone else they run as that user
2.15 · A database an interrupted run left invalid is dropped when the server next starts, saying so once, so it can be made again and connected to

capabilities.title: 3 · Dropping a throwaway test database
capabilities.description: Every package's tests drop the databases they made through this one module, which rides out Postgres's known refusals, instead of each package keeping its own copy.

contracts.title: 3.1 · Only a database named with a test token is dropped; any other name is refused before anything is sent to the server

3.2 · A drop ends the connections still open to the database, falls back to a plain DROP when Postgres refuses to end another backend, retries a bounded number of times while the database is still in use, and propagates every other error

capabilities.title: 1 · Scene layout
capabilities.description: Turns a project's stories and capabilities into a forest scene: islands and parcels on a hex lattice, trails between them and the props they carry, then maps that scene to 3D descriptors (src/core, src/scene.ts, src/world-to-3d.ts). *Noted in place, 2026-10-05 (ADR-0804 D1): the globe keeps only the scene's ground cells (each island's coast, parcels and reach); the trees, flora and props it still computes are drawn by nothing on a product surface.*

contracts.title: 1.1 · The same forest always builds byte-identical ground.
1.2 · The same input always gives the same trail network, and no visible trail runs into an island that is not its own.
1.3 · Every ground cell names its island, and a capability's cells name its parcel and wear its status.

capabilities.title: 2 · Island ground
capabilities.description: Builds each island's ground for the globe: its relaxed parcel cells and the coast rims clipped from them, drawn in exact colour. *Noted in place, 2026-10-06: the stepped cliff edge and the banded ground shader with its grass, sand, wheat, rock, wear and shadow layers left with the flat canvas (ADR-0920); the shore band and the land's fall to its waterline left with the last road that stood on them (increment_1c39930c645a). Only the waterline's dip (SHORE_DIP) and the relief's height bound (landHeightRange) remain, sizing the plates' clearance above the shell.*

contracts.title: 2.3 · The ground is drawn in exact colour (no output transform, no tone curve, no input conversion), and a canvas with any one of the three wrong is not exact colour.

capabilities.title: 3 · The canvas
capabilities.description: The React-Three-Fiber canvas that hosts the globe: it says when it is ready, frames the camera, reuses prepared ground when the scene has not changed, and draws on demand, including under a camera another canvas drives. PlanetWorldCanvas is the live canvas; the flat ForestWorldCanvas and its evidence page were deleted under ADR-0920.

contracts.title: 3.7 · A road is never thicker on screen as you zoom out, and never vanishes.
3.8 · Left alone, the globe draws no frame over 50 ms (verified by the Mint box's lag run)
3.9 · An animating glass sheet redraws its glass without re-deriving a shader program

capabilities.title: 4 · The planet
capabilities.description: Draws the world on a globe: each island a flat plate standing on the sphere at its spot, a glass globe whose far side is hidden, and trail ribbons running between the plates (src/planet).

contracts.title: 4.1 · Each island is a flat plate tangent to the big sphere at its spot (the glass sheet is its near pole), with its low ground above the sphere.
4.4 · Every recorded capability link between islands is one unbroken road across the glass, from dock to dock; a link within an island has none.
4.5 · An island on the globe is one ground surface with a coast line on each rim, lying on the globe's sphere, and marks laid on its land sit on that surface.
4.6 · A sideways CSS-pixel offset moves the glass sheet's perspective picture by that many pixels without moving or turning the eye.
4.7 · The map independently hides its island grounds and roads while keeping its camera and mounted plate children; hiding the whole exterior still preserves its inside.

4.8 · A lit link's lane is one unbroken strip from its capability's territory on the island built on, along its road between islands, to its capability's territory on the island building on it, following only lines drawn on each island; it is a thread of one width down the middle of its road, narrower than the narrowest road, with a soft glow in its colour that lanes sharing a stretch lay once between them, upstream blue and downstream violet, with a small mark in its colour at each end; where both colours share a road or an end, they remain distinguishable side by side

4.9 · Every lane of a selection starts at once and grows from its start by physical distance at one steady pace in its animation clock, so the selection settles in its longest lane's time; one warm head shows per shared stretch of one colour, slow frames preserve visible growth, and reduced motion shows every lane whole immediately with no head
4.10 · The globe draws nothing while its canvas is off screen, and draws again as soon as any of it is back
4.11 · An island facing the viewer hides whatever lies behind it, and nothing laid on its own land; an island seen from behind, through the glass, hides nothing

4.12 · A road between islands follows the globe's surface: no stretch of it cuts through the glass or rises above the islands' land, and it ends on its island's coast as drawn, however far round the globe its islands sit
4.13 · A capability link naming a capability on no island is left out on its own: every other road is still drawn, and the notice names what was left out
4.14 · A road to islands far round the globe is routed up to their coast: the chart it is routed on is centred on the islands, so none is stretched far past its coast and no road stops short of it
4.15 · When the browser hands the globe's drawing context back, the globe draws itself again, as it was

4.16 · Live roads grow by distance from dependency to dependent on first display and arrival; established shared roads stay drawn, unrelated updates preserve progress, and reduced motion shows the complete roads immediately

4.17 · Showing a hidden roads surface draws its pathways by distance from dependency to dependent over one second; rerenders preserve progress, recorded arrivals remain authoritative, and reduced motion shows the permitted roads immediately
4.19 · A road may end on an island as a whole, named by its story, as well as on a capability on it
4.21 · A layout draws its islands at once and its roads when routed, off the page's main thread where the page offers a road worker; an overtaken routing draws nothing
4.22 · On the glass sheet each island stands at the place on the sheet it is given and faces the eye square-on, within a degree, and the eye's depth range stays tight around the sheet
4.23 · On the glass sheet every island is a raised plate of one shared thickness, its sides running from its land down to the glass, so it reads as solid land standing on the glass (ADR-1059 D2)
4.24 · On the glass sheet a hollow island is its coast line alone, hiding nothing beneath it, and turns solid again (ADR-1061 D2)

4.25 · Under smoked glass (the Stories look) what hangs under the glass sheet shows by the angle: hidden from well above, at the top resting tilt, in view from near level and from below, drawn behind the glass from above and over it from below (ADR-1062 D4)

4.26 · The glass sheet is seen in perspective: nearer is drawn bigger, a zoom moves the eye toward the middle of the view and reads back as the zoom asked for, and the sheet stays between the near and far planes (ADR-1062 D1)
4.27 · The glass sheet is a lit slab: the glass has a visible thickness with a rim round both faces, and its edge and every island's sides are shaded by the scene's lights (ADR-1062 D1)

4.28 · Under clear glass (the Library look) what hangs beneath the glass sheet shows at every angle, from straight above to straight below, and the glass clears and smokes again without moving (ADR-1062 D3, D4)
4.29 · A plumbing call is drawn as a road between the two islands it joins, one per kind
4.30 · A plumbing road is not a dependency: it joins no capability link, widens no road and lights no lane
4.31 · Each plumbing road is labelled at its middle with its kind's words only, never a value word
4.32 · A plumbing road reads as a different kind of road from a dependency
4.33 · In a recorded growth a plumbing road shows once both its islands have risen, never before
4.34 · A layout's plumbing roads are routed and kept like its capability roads
4.35 · DOM laid over the sheet (a plumbing label, the roads notice) shows whenever the sheet opens, again included, and unmounts no React root while React renders

capabilities.title: 5 · Growth
capabilities.description: The globe replays a recorded sequence of plan states as growth: islands rise, roads draw on with the dependency-lane motion, and parts and files fill in, at a chosen speed.

contracts.title: 5.1 · A growth replays only what the recording holds, in its stages' order, and roads only leave risen islands
5.2 · A whole globe grows from a point of light to its full form in the length asked for, keeping order and pacing
5.3 · An island rises from its middle without overshoot, its parts and files filling in behind it; reduced motion shows the end at once
5.4 · The globe given a growth hides what has not risen, draws roads on from their built-on end, and ends identical to the globe without one
5.5 · A recorded date falls in the replay where it fell between the dated stages, so dates keep their order
5.6 · A stage that holds a beat for what it carries beyond the plan takes that beat, even when it adds nothing
5.7 · A host scrubbing a growth to a fixed moment sees that moment even under reduced motion

openWork.arcTitle: Capability tree: a map of capabilities, their interfaces, and the work landing on them
openWork.title: Session file reads on the land after the dots: show them another way, or delete the unfed traversal code

capabilities.title: 1 · Button and composer
capabilities.description: The corner button and the composer it opens: above every canvas, Ctrl+Shift+F, a surface chip correctable from the declared list, required text, Sent only after the write returns, and a failure that keeps the text with Retry and Copy.

contracts.title: 1.1 · The corner button, or Ctrl+Shift+F, starts a pick above whatever is open, and the composer opens on the picked element's surface, which can be corrected from the declared list
1.2 · Send needs text, a picked element and a surface, and says Sent only after the write returns, with the element and its picture
1.3 · A failed write keeps the text and offers Retry and Copy

1.4 · While picking, the element under the pointer is outlined with its tag and size, a click attaches it without pressing it, Escape before the first pick leaves nothing open and Escape from Pick again returns to the note, and neither the corner nor a drawn canvas is picked

capabilities.title: 2 · Surface naming
capabilities.description: Which named surface is in front: the resolver reads the canvases marked with a declared id and picks the top-most (an open popover or dialog, then an overlay, then a side panel, then the main view), and the declared list it is checked against.

contracts.title: 2.1 · The top-most named surface on show is recorded: an open popover or dialog, then an overlay, then a side panel, then the main view; none on show names none

2.2 · The element pointed at is recorded with a selector only it matches, its tag, role, accessible name, text, marks, React components, box, styles and markup capped at 2 KB with only allowlisted attributes and secrets redacted, in its nearest surface; an icon is picked as its control, and a drawn canvas and the corner never are

capabilities.title: 3 · Feedback record
capabilities.description: The main process's side: a capture of the app window taken before the composer opens, and the feedback record written into project storytree with its screenshot, through this package's own page channels.

contracts.title: 3.1 · Sending writes one feedback record in project storytree with the text, surface, its story, the element it points at, selection, project viewed, version, window size, theme, time and status new
3.2 · The app window is captured before the composer opens and stored as a JPEG with the record, unless the owner drops it; the button is offered only where the library holds project storytree
3.3 · A picture cut to the element, widened by a margin, is captured once the element is picked and stored beside the window's picture; dropping the pictures drops both

capabilities.title: 4 · Triage
capabilities.description: The `storytree feedback` commands the two-hourly session manager triages the owner's feedback notes with: list the new ones, read one whole with its screenshot, and mark one routed to an increment, a question, or a reasoned close.

contracts.title: 4.1 · `feedback list` shows each new feedback note, oldest first, with its id, time, surface, story and text, and whether it has a screenshot; routed notes only with --all, each with its route

4.2 · `feedback route <feedback> --to increment|question|closed --reason` marks a new note routed with its route, target and reason; an increment or question target must be a live record of that kind, an already routed note or a non-feedback id is refused with nothing written

4.3 · `feedback show <feedback> [--screenshot <file>]` prints the note whole with the element it points at and, given a file, writes its screenshot JPEG there and the element's crop beside it; a note sent without one says so

capabilities.title: 1 · The address and its guards
capabilities.description: The door's one web address, which claude.ai calls from Anthropic's infrastructure through a public tunnel, and the guards that keep strangers and floods off it: a secret route, a bare 404 everywhere else, the caller's address range, a Host list, body and batch limits, child limits and timeouts, and a keep-alive longer than the tunnel's.

contracts.title: 1.1 · A request to any path but /mcp/<secret> (/.well-known/* and /mcp/<wrong secret> included) is answered 404 with an empty body, never 401, and reaches no tool.
1.2 · On the secret route, any method but POST is answered 405 with Allow: POST and an empty body.

1.3 · With caller ranges configured, a request on the secret route whose X-Forwarded-For last hop (the one the tunnel adds) is missing, not an IP address, or outside every range is answered 403 and runs no tool; one inside a range is served, whatever entries the caller put before it.
1.4 · A request on the secret route whose Host is neither localhost nor a configured host is refused before any tool runs.

1.5 · A body over 64 KB, whether declared in Content-Length or found while reading, is answered 413 and the connection closed only after the rest is drained, so the client sees 413 rather than a reset; a body under it is served.
1.6 · A JSON-RPC batch (a body whose first non-blank character is "[") is answered 400 with JSON-RPC error -32600 and runs none of its calls.

1.7 · At most 2 storytree children and 4 git children run at once; up to 4 and 8 more calls wait for a slot at most one full command and its kill grace (25 + 2 = 27 s, ADR-1163 D3), and any call beyond that, or waiting longer, gets a "busy, try again" tool error without starting a child.

1.8 · A child that runs past its time limit (25 s for a storytree command, 30 s for a library search, 15 s for git) is stopped, and its call answers a tool error naming the limit, inside the client's 60 s request timeout.
1.9 · A caller hanging up before its answer stops that call's child, or takes the call out of the queue, and frees its slot.
1.10 · An idle connection stays open for 100 s, longer than the tunnel's 90 s pool: a second request on the same socket after 95 s idle is served, not refused.

1.11 · The door refuses to start, with a plain message and exit code 1, when its secret is missing, shorter than 32 characters or holds anything but letters, digits, "-" and "_", when its repository folder is not readable, or when a caller range is not a CIDR.

1.12 · Every child the door starts is given an argument array with no shell, runs in the door's repository copy, and inherits only PATH, HOME, LANG, TZ, STORYTREE_HOME, the temp folder and Windows' basics: none of the door's secret, settings or other variables, and a "$" or ";" in a caller's words reaches the child as plain text.

1.13 · Every storytree child runs with STORYTREE_SESSION_ID set to a voice session id (voice-YYYY-MM-DD) and no other harness's session id, so whatever it records names a voice session, never the owner.
1.14 · The door's log never holds the secret, the request path or a tool's arguments: each request is one line of method, tool name, status, time taken and caller address.
1.15 · With no sign-in service configured, no signed tool is registered and the sign-in metadata path is a bare 404; sign-in settings come all together or the door refuses to start

1.16 · With sign-in configured, GET /.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/mcp/<secret> answers protected-resource metadata naming the connector's exact address and the sign-in service; every other well-known path stays a bare 404

1.17 · A signed tool's call with no token, or a token that fails its signature, issuer, audience (the connector's exact address) or expiry, is 401 with a Bearer challenge naming the metadata, and runs no tool
1.18 · A valid token for anyone but the owner's own user id is 403; the owner's valid token runs the signed tool, which knows it is him
1.19 · Reads never look at the token: with sign-in configured, a read with no token, a bad one or an expired one is served, and even unreachable sign-in keys take no read down

1.20 · With VOICE_SIGNIN_EVERY_CALL=1, every call without the owner's token, initialize and reads included, is 401 with the sign-in challenge; the owner's token is served and anyone else's is 403; unset or 0, reads stay open.
1.21 · A tool call whose arguments hold more than 100 array elements and object members is refused before any tool runs, and a subscription stream is refused at once rather than held open.

capabilities.title: 2 · The read tools
capabilities.description: What the owner can ask by voice: catch_up (what needs him), tell_me (one thing whole), find, what_changed, count, search_code and read_code, each read-only and answered in one call. The first increment's one-record reads, show_question and read_note, gave way to tell_me (increment_2817aed6f216).

contracts.title: 27.1 · library count tallies live records by kind and status, and open increments by arc, leaving health out
27.2 · library changes lists the latest changes newest first by sequence number, at most 20, health left out
27.3 · library find lists live records whose title holds every word, at most 20, long titles cut
27.4 · library read takes a decision's number, 1103 or ADR-1103, in place of its id

27.5 · library changes --actor <writer> lists every record the writer wrote, health left out, by id: created, updated by N writes, or retired with its reason, each changed field from before their first write to after their last, and the first later writer and entry where another wrote since; it takes no --limit.
2.1 · tools/list offers exactly the read tools, each annotated read-only and not destructive, and no tool that writes.

2.2 · catch_up returns what needs the owner's action (owner waits, work blocked on him), in arc waits' rank order, each saying its rank and its why before its note, then one line on the event waits naming each overdue one, then his open questions arc by arc (the arcs in the order of their oldest question, oldest first within each), then what landed since a given time, or, with none given, since he last heard (the point mark_heard keeps after the whole read-out, 5.11), else the last 24 hours, in that order, each item numbered with its record id at the line's end; then, with writes on, what has happened since he last heard to what his voice notes became (5.11, 2.22); then the FYIs he has not heard, oldest first, unnumbered, each with when, what happened and its id. Its action list holds only what arc waits lists for him (no wait on a parked arc) and closes with one line counting the waits it left out on parked arcs. A question another session is putting to him now is left out and counted, and, with writes on, one he answered by voice that waits for the manager is named as answered, not offered.
2.6 · find returns at most 5 library records closest in meaning to the owner's words, one line each with its kind, title and record id.

2.7 · find passes its query to the search as words only: one beginning with "--" finds records instead of setting a flag, and an empty query, one over 500 characters or one holding a NUL is refused with a tool error before any child runs.

2.8 · what_changed with a span from its fixed list returns the increments closed in that span grouped by arc, each with its pull request, at most 20 rows; a span not on the list is refused with a tool error naming the spans it takes.
2.9 · what_changed with a record id returns that record's history, newest first, at most 20 entries, each with when, who and what changed.

2.10 · search_code finds an exact piece of text, not a pattern, in the committed HEAD of the door's repository copy, never its working tree: at most 60 lines as path:line: text, at most 5 per file, each cut to 300 characters, saying when more were left out.

2.11 · search_code and read_code refuse a path that is absolute, starts with "~", holds ":" or "..", or resolves outside the repository, and search_code refuses empty or multi-line text; text or a path beginning with "-" is searched for, never read as a git option.
2.12 · read_code returns up to 300 numbered lines, at most 15,000 characters, of one file as committed at HEAD, from start_line (1 if not given), and says which start_line continues it when it cut.

2.13 · read_code refuses, with a short tool error, a path HEAD does not hold as a file (missing, a folder, a symbolic link), a binary file, a file over 5 MB, a start_line past the file's end and an end_line before start_line.
2.14 · A read that fails or is refused answers a short plain tool error with no stack trace, and a read that succeeds carries none of the command line's "next:" commands or colour codes.

2.15 · tell_me reads one thing whole by a spoken handle: a question with its stakes, then its recommendation, then its options, a decision by number, an arc, an increment or pull request, a research result or a term
2.16 · count gives the library's fixed tallies (live records by kind and status) and the arcs with the most open increments, from the library's own count, taking no query
2.17 · find tries titles first (the library's title lookup, a decision by its number) and searches by meaning only when no title holds the words

2.19 · the instructions a client gets on connect follow the shared briefing (pattern_5ab3b3241c67): open with catch_up's actions and event-wait line alone and wait for "move on", then the questions in catch_up's order, then what landed, what changed since he last heard and the FYIs; they name no tool tools/list does not offer; the write rules (save notes in his words, his done actions included, mark each question being put to him, mark heard what he has heard, offer to send them to the manager) come only with writes on

2.20 · the instructions carry the shared briefing (pattern_5ab3b3241c67) whole, from a committed file generated from the note (`pnpm build:briefing`), never from the library at start-up; `pnpm check:briefing` fails while the committed file differs from the note, and an edited note, rebuilt, changes both these instructions and the grill-me skill

2.21 · catch_up reads an answer's state from the library: answered by voice while its note waits to be routed, taken by a run or not, and offered again once the note is routed with its question still open

2.22 · `voice since`, run as the door's role, gives what each question, increment or arc a routed voice note's outcome names has come to since the point he last heard: an open increment as open, or in progress with the pull requests that landed on it, never parked; one landed since then with its pull request, one unchanged since then left out; before any mark, all of them

2.23 · tell_me reads an open increment as open, or in progress with the pull requests that landed on it, never parked, leading with why it exists (its body's opening sentence) and who proposed it (its history's first writer)

capabilities.title: 3 · The speech layer
capabilities.description: Follow-ups the owner can say aloud: spoken references such as "decision eleven-oh-three" and "number two" resolve to one record, two or more matches answer "which one?" with at most three names and act on none, answers stay short with "say more" pages, and record ids are never read aloud.

contracts.title: 3.1 · A decision or pull-request number said as words ("eleven-oh-three", "seventeen twenty-three", "eleven hundred and three", "one one oh three") or as digits resolves to that number
3.2 · "Number two" (an ordinal, said or as a digit) names the item catch_up numbers 2, in catch_up's fixed order, so a position heard in catch_up names the same item in a follow-up
3.3 · A handle two or more records match answers "which one?" with at most three names, reads none of them, and speaks no id
3.4 · A spoken answer is at most 2,000 words a page, with "say more" pages, and holds no record id except at a line's end
3.5 · On a named arc, voice lists its open increments numbered a page at a time, and "number three" reads that increment whole

capabilities.title: 4 · The box service and its confinement
capabilities.description: Running the door on the Mint box confined: its own box user, its own repository copy refreshed by a timer, its own narrow database role, and system service limits, so the internet-facing process holds none of the owner's keys or superuser login.

contracts.title: 4.1 · The refresh fast-forwards the door's copy to main, reinstalls only on a lockfile change, restarts only when HEAD moved, and puts HEAD back when an install fails

4.2 · The install gives the door its own copy and units reading the spike's secret env file, enables only the refresh timer, changes nothing on --dry-run, and refuses the pool's checkout (agent-pool.json) as its copy

4.3 · The door's database role, granted exactly its grant files, answers every read the door's tools make through the real command line, and is refused every write to the library, its history, the activity log, transcripts, screenshots and the trunks; its one library write, adding voice.note records, is storytree's fence from voice's manifest (4.11), never these files
4.4 · The door's role may add to the search cache but never change or remove what is in it
4.5 · Voice can turn its writes off but never back on: the lock is a row the door's role may add and never remove, and only the box's own account clears it

4.6 · The confined units run the door as its own system user with no view of home folders, no new privileges and a 3 GB memory cap, and its refresh asks for a restart through a request file rather than any privilege of its own
4.7 · The confined door's env file carries only the door's own settings (its secret, PORT, ALLOWED_HOSTS, ALLOWED_CIDRS), never a path the unit sets itself
4.8 · the box's listener survives losing its database connection: it reconnects, catches up with a tick, and goes on starting confirmed runs

4.9 · voice's listener (run always) and committer (run every 15 minutes) are services its manifest declares, which the service host runs: each starts with the host's handle and ends when its stop signal fires

4.10 · the door runs the code the part switch names: the factory plugin standing in for voice while switched to one, none otherwise, since storytree's base ships no voice (voice-host part voice on is refused, naming plugin voice); its refresh keeps storytree's copy and the factory clone at main, points the door's link at the plugin, and restarts once when anything moved

4.11 · the door's role, fenced by storytree as voice's manifest declares it (`storytree plugin fence`: voice.note and voice.mark, each written by storytree_voice), adds voice.note and voice.mark records and is refused any other kind, an update and a delete

4.12 · voice-host refresh-status, run as the box user, reads systemd's record of the refresh and reports it FAILED, quoting what its last run printed, and exits 1 when that run failed, its timer is not active, or it last ran over an hour ago; otherwise it reads ok

capabilities.title: 5 · Drafted writes with read-back and undo
capabilities.description: The writes voice may make: save_note keeps what the owner says at once as a note, answers included (ADR-1155); start_manager_run is a draft read back in one line and, once confirmed, handed to the box at once by a database notification (ADR-1155 D3), carrying every unswept note to the run; confirm, cancel (until the run starts) and lock_voice. Every write is recorded as a voice session, never as the owner. None is registered until sign-in and confinement land.

dependsOn.title: 4 · The box service and its confinement

contracts.title: 5.1 · The write tools exist only with sign-in, each needs the owner's token, and while voice_lock holds a row every one refuses and writes nothing

stories.title: The library
stories.description: The library is storytree's knowledge management: where one project's records live, how they are stored and how they are kept honest (ADR-1066 D4). It holds the plan of work (stories, arcs, increments and the owner's questions), how healthy each piece is, and what the project has learned. Its storage is Postgres: on this computer it runs on The local database, its own story since ADR-1076, which its tests use too; the keys a user gives storytree are Keys' own story, which it calls (ADR-1075). Its curation tooling is what the librarian-curator role uses on its pass at a landing: new artifacts genuinely new, links to what they rest on, every accepted decision true, durable lessons graduated and lapsed questions reviewed (capabilities 21 to 26, once The librarian, ADR-1077 D3); it files and routes no friction, which is Friction's own story. Every other story reads and writes it only through its API; people see it through the map view and the work board, and agents reach it through the agent tools. Its code lives in packages/library (the librarian in src/librarian).

capabilities.title: 1 · Project libraries
capabilities.description: Each project gets its own library, a separate database on one Postgres server, created the first time the project is opened, with its tables set up automatically, and brought up to date by the next open after storytree adds to them. Opening a project whose tables are already current touches no table, so an account let only read, or write a few kinds of record, can open it too. Storytree can list the projects on the server, and nothing written in one project can ever show up in another, with one exception: a product project names the user's factory, and reads its system (roles, notes and checks) from it, its own records of the same kind and title winning (ADR-1040).

contracts.title: 1.1 · `openProject("site")` on a server with no storytree databases creates the project's database and its tables; a project set up before a table changed gains what was added since at its next open.
1.2 · Opening the same project again succeeds and changes nothing (no error, no second database, its records are untouched).
1.3 · After opening "site" and "app", `listProjects()` returns exactly `["app", "site"]`. Databases on the server that are not storytree projects are never listed.
1.4 · A record saved in "site" cannot be read from "app".

1.5 · A project name that is not lower-case letters, digits and single hyphens (1–40 characters, starting with a letter or digit) is refused before anything touches the server, and the error names the rule.
1.6 · `snapshot("site")` returns every record of the project and its whole history, as they stood at one moment, while writes go on.

1.7 · `restore("copy", snapshot)` into a project with no records and no history gives back the same records and the same history, sequence numbers, actors and times included, and the next write continues after them.
1.8 · Restoring into a project that holds any record or any history is refused, naming the project, and writes nothing.

1.9 · A local database that accepts TCP but never completes a fresh handshake is refused at a 10-second connection deadline by default (ADR-1163 D1), or at the deadline the caller gives, for both the server and project pools, with an actionable "storytree isn't reachable" answer that says the database took longer than that to answer and the computer may be busy. This includes library opens made by the CLI. A later call recovers once the database answers.

1.10 · Opening a project whose tables are current runs no table setup and writes nothing, so an account that may only read its tables (not their owner, no right to create in its schema) opens it and reads its records.

1.11 · Opening a project whose tables are not current, as an account that may not change them (no CREATE on its schema, or not holding the owner's rights over its tables), changes nothing: no table statement runs and no memory is converted. A project set up before opens as its tables stand, reads and writes as the account's grants allow, and warns once per process per project, naming the project, the account and the role owning its database. A project never set up is refused with a ConnectionError (`project-owner`) naming the project and the account and saying that only the role owning its database may set it up. Its owner's next open sets the tables up as before.

1.12 · `dropProject(name)` deletes the project's database, with every record and all its history, for every machine using the server; it is listed no more, other projects are untouched, and an unknown project is refused. An open that only reaches an existing project (`openProject(name, { create: false })`, how a folder that names a project opens it) refuses a deleted one as gone and never makes it again.
1.13 · Closing a server connection waits for project and own-database openings already in flight, releases every pool they create, and refuses new openings once closing starts.

1.14 · Loopback database connections refuse cleartext and MD5 password requests before sending credential material, for both admin and project pools; SCRAM and passwordless test connections still work.
1.15 · A project records whether it is the user's factory or a product naming its factory, and refuses to be both
1.16 · A product project reads its factory's roles, notes and checks, and its own record of the same kind and title wins
1.17 · A product's link to a system record it retired reads the record of that kind and title: its own, else its factory's
1.18 · An edit through a product of a system record it reads from its factory writes the product's own copy, which wins, and retiring one hides it from the product; the factory is unchanged
1.19 · A product's inherited records are the factory's system records it reads and holds none of its own for

1.20 · A local url naming a connect_timeout (libpq's, in seconds) longer than the given deadline gives its handshakes that deadline, on both admin and project pools, and the refusal says so; a url naming none, or a shorter one, keeps the given deadline (10 seconds by default)

1.21 · A project opened with system switches leaves each switched-off role, check and note out of its lists, selections and searches, a product's factory's included; a record's own title or id beats its group, which beats all; reading one by its id still finds it, and the plan is never switched off
1.22 · Each history entry carries the server's own time and the account that wrote it, and no writer may change or remove one
1.23 · An outside writer's role, fenced to its plugin's kinds, inserts a record of its own kind, and each history entry carries its role in recorded_by
1.24 · An outside writer's role is refused a core kind, another plugin's kind, an update, a delete and any change to the tables
1.25 · An outside writer whose plugin declares updates may change its own kind's records, and still no other record nor another kind
1.26 · A project opened with a plugin's kinds writes and reads them; opened without them, a record of that kind reads dormant
1.27 · fenceProject fences a plugin's writers in a live project's library as the owner, refusing a missing role or a non-owner account and naming what it fenced first
1.28 · A change to the history goes only through the logged repair switch, for the owner too, and the owner's ordinary writes pass when row-level security is forced
1.29 · A shared library gets schema and own-database table statements only from merged code

capabilities.title: 2 · Library transactions
capabilities.description: The only data actions the library allows are: save a record, fetch it, list records of one type, change only named fields, retire a record with a reason, revert a record, retired or not, to the state one of its own history entries kept, or revert every record one writer wrote to its state before that writer's first write, refused where another writer wrote since. Every change is all-or-nothing, and is written first to a permanent, append-only history, so nothing is ever truly erased.

contracts.title: 2.1 · `save` creates a record. Saving the same id again replaces it, and each save appends one history entry.
2.2 · `edit` changes only the fields it names; every other field keeps its stored value.
2.3 · `edit` merges onto what is stored NOW, not onto a copy the caller read earlier. If two edits of different fields race, both survive.
2.4 · `edit` of a missing record returns `null` and creates nothing.
2.5 · `get` of a missing record returns `null` and never throws.
2.6 · `list(type)` returns only that type's current records (none retired), and `[]` when there are none.
2.7 · `retire(id, reason)` removes the record from `get`/`list`, keeps the reason in the history, and retiring an already-retired or missing record is a harmless no-op.

2.8 · `history()` returns every change in the order it happened, with strictly increasing sequence numbers. `history({ id })` filters to one record, and `history({ since })` returns only entries after that sequence number.
2.9 · A `validate` check passed to `save`/`edit` sees the merged result. If it throws, nothing is written (no record change and no history entry).

2.10 · A write naming an `actor` keeps it in history. A write without one is accepted and its history entry has no actor; an edit or retirement never inherits an earlier write's actor. Refused writes and harmless no-ops add no history entry.

2.11 · Save, edit and retire accept an optional abort signal. If aborted before write admission, including while waiting for the project write lock, they reject without changing records or history. After admission, cancellation does not interrupt the write or undo its history. The in-memory twin applies the same boundary at write entry.

2.12 · `history` also narrows on the server: `from` (a time) keeps the changes made at or after it, to the millisecond, however the time is written; `types` keeps only changes to records of those types (none for an empty list); `oldest: n` or `newest: n` keeps only the first or last n of what matches, still in order. Filters combine with each other and with `id` and `since`; a malformed one (a limit that is not a whole number above 0, both limits, or a time that is not one) is refused with a RangeError before anything is read.
2.13 · Lists narrow on the server by ids and stored field values, take an ordered limit, and project only requested fields on the named schema version; memory and Postgres agree.

2.14 · `revert(id, to, read)` writes the record back to the state its own history entry `to` kept, whole: changed fields restored, removed ones put back, added ones gone. It is one more `updated` entry whose reason names the entry it reverts to, with its writer; nothing in history is rewritten.

2.15 · A revert of a retired record to an entry before its retirement brings it back live under its own id, created when it first was, so links to that id reconnect. A retirement entry is not a state to revert to.

2.16 · A revert is refused, writing nothing, when the record was written to after the entry the writer read (`read` is not its newest seq), when the entry is not the record's own, or when its validate check throws.
2.17 · `history({ actor })` keeps only the changes one writer made, as their entries name them, on the server, combined with the other filters.

2.18 · `revertWrites({ of })` writes every record `of` wrote (health left out) back, in one write, to its state before `of`'s first write to it: a changed record to its entry before, a record `of` retired live again, a record `of` made retired. Each is one more entry naming the writer reverted and the entry it goes back to, with its own writer and reason; a record `of` made and retired itself is left alone. It returns what it changed, by id.

2.19 · `revertWrites` is refused, writing nothing, when another writer (named or not) wrote to any record `of` wrote after `of`'s first write to it: LaterWriterError names each such record with the first such entry and its writer. A check that throws refuses it whole too.
2.20 · A write made for a writer who had read outside text keeps what it read in its history entry; a write without one carries no mark
2.21 · A library whose history has no place for the outside-text mark yet writes and reads its history as before, leaving the mark off
2.22 · Each history entry read back names the account the server saw write it

2.23 · `history({ actions })` keeps only the changes of those actions (created, updated, retired), on the server, combined with the other filters; none for an empty list, and an action no change has is refused with a RangeError before anything is read.
2.24 · inOneWrite commits every write its work makes together, or none when the work throws

capabilities.title: 3 · Data schema
