capabilities.title: 1 · Get storytree
capabilities.description:
One command gets the Windows app and the tools its agent needs onto the computer, ready to run without a storytree checkout. Running it again reuses a working installation or explains what failed and how to retry.

As built: the release publishes install-storytree.ps1, its PowerShell one-liner and a version-matched SHA-256 manifest alongside the existing combined Windows x64/arm64 NSIS installer. Desktop packaging ships a native pinned Node 24 runtime, the complete agent-link buildBins output including imported chunks, a delivery helper and Node's license in resources/agent-tools. Delivery verifies and reuses a working installation before contacting the feed, explicitly launches its executable to show a hidden window or establish the first app launch, and waits for the app-owned database. It records stable installed tool paths in the 0.3 home's delivery.json and puts its CLI wrapper on the per-user Windows PATH; unrelated storytree commands are preserved and named. Failed steps include a retry action, incomplete existing apps are retained with repair/update instructions, and delivery does not create projects, change harness settings, install a developer toolchain, or touch 0.2. Ordinary updates remain the app's existing NSIS update route and replace the tool payload at the same paths. setup install retains its existing hook/command meaning; capability 2 owns connection.

Evidence: packages/app-setup/evidence/deliver/README.md. Linux tests use temporary homes, fake app launch/readiness and real PowerShell orchestration with injected effects; the actual built CLI, hook, setup, delivery helper and MCP server run outside a checkout. Both Windows runtime downloads match pinned SHA-256 values and their PE architectures. Windows CI additionally checks the installed x64 tool payload from a path with spaces. These proofs do not attest real first-ever/hidden-window startup, fresh-terminal registry propagation, interrupted NSIS installation, native arm64 execution, a live release update with active agent processes, or the agent-link 8.6 two-harness walkthrough; those remain the laptop acceptance lane.

As built (ADR-1162, contract 1.15): once delivery is ready the one-liner asks nothing. Its first line after the install says the app is open and gives the terminal command that opens it again; connecting agents and adding a project are the app's first-run guide (capability 3). `storytree setup connect` still connects from a terminal through delivery.json and capability 2's registration functions. Tools registration is never presented as hooks verified. Evidence of the earlier prompt: packages/app-setup/evidence/join/README.md.

As built (ADR-0854): on Windows the installed command is `storytree.exe`, a 5 KB program of its own built with LLVM from the agent link's launcher source and shipped in the payload as `storytree-launcher.exe`, so no shell reads its words: from Git Bash, Windows PowerShell or a program that starts it, each word reaches the CLI as the caller's command line spelled it (contract 1.9). The batch file it was before, `storytree.cmd`, is replaced by it in its folder. Evidence: packages/app-setup/evidence/native-launcher/README.md.

As built (groundwork for the macOS arc, arc_5b467265f126, contract 1.11): the delivery API also stages Apple Silicon's runtime. `macRuntime("arm64")` pins Node 24.21.0's darwin-arm64 archive and its bin/node hash, and `stageRuntime` extracts that executable with mode 755, refusing any checksum mismatch and keeping the previous runtime. `writePayloadManifest` takes the platform: a Mac payload needs `node` and no Windows launcher. `toolPaths`/`verifyPayload` read a .app bundle's Contents/Resources/agent-tools and Contents/MacOS/storytree-0.3. macOS packaging, the shell install and notarisation are the arc's later increments. Evidence: packages/app-setup/evidence/deliver/README.md.

As built (Linux arc, arc_38613dac8d7c, contract 1.13): the same curl | sh one-liner installs on x64 Linux. install.sh refuses another chip, installs where FUSE cannot be used (no libfuse2, or a /dev/fuse this user cannot open) and runs the app unpacked there with APPIMAGE_EXTRACT_AND_RUN=1, saying so (it never runs sudo), takes the release's AppImage by its checksum from storytree-delivery.json's linux.x64 entry, and installs a folder ~/.local/share/storytree-0.3 holding the AppImage as storytree-0.3, its resources/agent-tools extracted beside it (so toolPaths(dir, "linux") reads it unchanged and the hooks' Node path stays put) and its icon, plus a menu entry in ~/.local/share/applications whose Exec starts the installed AppImage with the arguments the release packaged. The installed version is read from the AppImage's own desktop entry (X-AppImage-Version), extracted without FUSE. The PATH line goes in ~/.profile; the command itself is the helper's ~/.storytree/0.3/bin/storytree, as on a Mac. The helper runs from x64 Linux's payload. The Linux release runner writes storytree-delivery-linux.json, merged into the manifest on publish. Not proved here: a launch and database start in a real desktop session, and the Ubuntu 24.04 sandbox question; those are the Mint acceptance increment's.

contracts.title: 1.1 · On a clean Windows x64 machine and an arm64 machine, the PowerShell one-line command delivers the matching app, a bundled Node runtime and a runnable tool-server, hook, setup and command-line bundle, including its imported chunks.

1.2 · The first-run journey displays the app and reaches its database both without a previous launch record and when the app is already running with its window hidden, without a separate manual "open once" step.
1.3 · Repeating the command in the same or a second folder reuses the installation without replacing user settings or touching 0.2's installation or data, and creates no project.
1.4 · An interrupted or refused installation reports the failed step and a retry action, without announcing a working connection or replacing the last usable installation.

1.5 · After the app takes an ordinary release update, the next agent session still starts compatible tools from a durable location, without rebuilding a checkout or relying on a package-manager cache.
1.6 · The installed command runs from a fresh Windows terminal; an existing unrelated `storytree` command is preserved and the conflict is named.

1.8 · Uninstalling from Windows Apps & features (or `storytree setup uninstall`) removes everything storytree added. That is the app, its command and PATH entry, this installation's agent registrations, hooks and status line in Claude Code and Codex, the update cache and its home. It asks first whether to keep the local library (kept, only the library stays). The user's project folders, other agent settings and another installation's home stay untouched, and an app update removes nothing.

1.9 · On Windows, the installed command hands each word on as the caller's command line spelled it, through no shell: run by name from Git Bash, Windows PowerShell or a program that starts it, a word holding >, &, |, % or ^ arrives unchanged, as does an inner double quote from Git Bash or a program; nothing else runs and no file is written (ADR-0854; proven on Windows CI, skipped with a named reason elsewhere).
1.10 · First-user delivery selects the pinned stable build, alpha requires an explicit choice, and a repeat preserves the installation channel before launch

1.11 · On an Apple Silicon Mac, the tool payload carries a pinned, checksum-verified darwin-arm64 Node runtime staged executable, lives in the .app bundle's Contents, needs its node and no Windows launcher, and refuses a missing or damaged file; on x64 Linux it carries the pinned linux-x64 runtime the same way, under the AppImage's resources; Windows payloads keep their own requirements (each runtime is run on its own system's CI, skipped with a named reason elsewhere)

1.12 · On an Apple Silicon Mac, `curl -fsSL …/install-storytree.sh | sh` (POSIX sh, also under bash or zsh) refuses any other system or chip in plain words, takes the channel's release, refuses a Mac app whose checksum does not match, installs it to ~/Applications, puts the command on PATH through one marked ~/.zprofile line written once, then asks nothing and says how to open the app, as the Windows one-liner does (1.15); run again over an app older than the channel's release, it says so and replaces the app, keeping ~/.storytree, and over the current one it changes nothing
1.13 · The x64 Linux one-liner: the same curl | sh installs the AppImage without admin rights
1.14 · On Linux and macOS, the one-liner makes storytree's home readable by its owner alone (0700), and the release channel record it saves there 0600

1.15 · Once it has installed, the one-line command (Windows, macOS, Linux) asks nothing: no agent connection, no project folder, no default taken from the folder it ran from. Its first words after the install say the app is open and give the command that opens it again from a terminal (ADR-1162 D1, D2).

1.16 · When the finish step cannot bring the app up, it keeps the launched app's output and names the cause (Electron refusing root without --no-sandbox, /dev/fuse unusable, initdb refusing root, no display), with the output's file, instead of a bare timeout

1.17 · The stable routine on the Mint box runs, and reports a run it could not make: it approves its own clone when refused as unapproved, files any other refusal or a judge's missing verdict as a harness friction (never a build's regression), counts a fortnight only once a build was judged, and its judge signs in with the routine's token

capabilities.title: 2 · Connect an agent
capabilities.description:
The user chooses Claude Code, Codex or both, and storytree connects its installed tools to those agents. The next session uses the existing setup check to ask about the project and show whether the connection actually works.

As built: @storytree/app-setup/connect exports connectAgents and disconnectAgents for the chosen harnesses, with installedToolServerCommand(bundledNodePath, installedMcpScriptPath) as the delivery seam. Registration is per user, keeps unrelated settings and old entries, uses the existing storytree MCP name, and reports incompatible entries without overwriting. It captures no project or working directory. Repeating it leaves the compatible entry untouched. Missing harnesses, invalid settings, missing installed tools and failed writes produce separate recovery results for each harness.

As built: disconnect removes the selected registration and only hooks matching this installation, preserving other commands in mixed groups and any other installation's hooks. It keeps the shared command until no connection remains and removes only the matching launcher. A disconnected harness stays disconnected: disconnect records it in the storytree home (disconnected-harnesses.json), and the setup check, run from the other harness's sessions, registers no hooks for it until Connect connects it again. Installation results distinguish tools registration from hooks not verified; the existing setup check owns project consent and received-event verification. Connect also registers the chosen harness's hooks (and Claude Code's status line), never the unchosen one's, so the first session after installing already runs the start hook that asks the setup question; before this, hooks arrived only when that first session's tool server ran the setup check, too late for its own start. Registering is still not verifying: results keep saying "hooks not verified" until the setup check has received each event.

contracts.title: 2.1 · Choosing either harness or both registers the installed tool server per user for the chosen harnesses, preserving other servers, settings and any existing 0.2 entry.
2.2 · A new agent session in the invoking folder, and later in another folder, reaches that folder's existing setup check rather than a fixed installer directory or a hard-coded project.
2.3 · Repeating registration leaves one effective storytree entry per chosen harness; an incompatible existing entry is explained instead of silently overwritten.
2.4 · A missing harness or an invalid settings file gets a specific recovery action and no success claim for that harness; a successful registration for the other harness is reported separately.

2.5 · Disconnecting one harness keeps the other's connection and the shared command working; removing all connections cleans up only storytree-owned registrations, hooks and command, keeping project libraries and unrelated settings.

2.6 · The installation result tells "tools connected" apart from "hooks verified"; a missing hook stays named by the existing setup check until its event is received. For Codex it says whether its hooks run or wait for the user to trust them, naming the one step while they wait, and, from an administrator terminal, that Codex cannot run commands from one.

2.9 · Codex, which hides a tool server's instructions and tools until the agent searches for them, is told through the AGENTS.md in its home to call check_setup before its first change in a storytree project, and to ignore storytree in any other folder: one marked section, written again changes nothing, the user's own text kept, removed exactly.

2.7 · A first build in a fresh folder leaves a true plan: a new user's Claude Code session, asked to set storytree up in an empty folder, makes it a project; later sessions there, asked over several turns to build something small with tests, leave the project's library holding the stories, capabilities and contracts they planned and an arc with its increments, a contract reported red then green, an increment closed as landed, and every claim they took ended, as storytree's own command reads them back

2.8 · Developer homes keep sign-in contents out of markers, create owner-only POSIX and Windows homes and sensitive files before copying sign-ins, scrub legacy plaintext markers on removal, and hand back a refreshed sign-in only when the original is unchanged and its file is private; conflicting refreshes preserve both sign-ins and refuse removal. A permission failure prevents new sign-in writes.

2.10 · Choosing Cursor registers the tool server in ~/.cursor/mcp.json and storytree's hooks in ~/.cursor/hooks.json, keeping every other server and hook; repeating changes nothing, disconnecting removes exactly what it added, and a machine without Cursor gets a recovery action, not a success

2.11 · Choosing Pi registers the tool server directly exposed in Pi's mcp.json, installs storytree's Pi extension and its AGENTS.md section, keeping everything else; disconnecting removes exactly those
2.12 · Connecting Antigravity CLI registers storytree's tool server in its mcp_config.json and storytree's hooks as one named entry in its hooks.json, keeping everything else

2.13 · The agents this computer runs (their command answers --version) are found, each said connected to this installation or not; one not installed is not offered, and another installation's entry is not this one connected.

capabilities.title: 3 · First-run guide
capabilities.description:
A short in-app guide tells the user what to do next, what storytree will ask, and what a working first project looks like. They can reopen it when adding another project or recovering from a connection problem.

As built: @storytree/app-setup/view mounts one Help entry outside the project surface, available with no project, either forest or a library error. First launch offers the guide; dismissal is remembered locally and Help reopens it. The guide covers the chosen agent, explicit project consent, harness approval, received-hook verification, first visible work, a second project, troubleshooting for the platform it runs on (contract 3.15: read from the renderer's user agent; Windows' unsigned installer and Smart App Control, macOS's Open Anyway, Linux's FUSE, root and desktop-session causes, and each platform's removal; every platform's when it cannot tell) and feedback. Since ADR-1162 the guide's first section sets up the computer, both steps optional: it lists each coding agent the computer runs (capability 2's agentsOnThisComputer), connected or with its own Connect, which connects through delivery.json's tools or the app's own, and offers Add a project… through the same folder picker as New project… (contract 3.13). Check a folder calls the agent link’s public runSetupCheck and displays its diagnostic lines and fixes. The adjacent copy action prepares a check_setup request for the agent; this folder check does not install hooks or the command and cannot verify hook receipt. The app’s existing projectSelection/followProjects refresh remains responsible for the project list.

Evidence: packages/app-setup/evidence/help/README.md. Headless Chromium exercises the actual renderer and isolated library, including two setup fixtures and both selectable forests. Contract 3.3’s real two-empty-folder/two-yes harness walkthrough and the final installer handoff remain Windows acceptance work.

contracts.title: 3.1 · Completing installation offers the in-app guide without requiring a project to exist, and its entry point opens it again later.
3.2 · From the guide, the user can reach the existing setup diagnostics and their recovery action when the connection is incomplete.

3.3 · The guide says how to add a project three ways (the app's Add project, `storytree doctor --set-up <name>` in a terminal, or asking the agent in the folder); a project added any of these ways appears in the running app and both forests are selectable.

3.4 · Add project in the app's Projects section or the first-run guide, or started from the app bar's "New project…", opens the native folder picker; the chosen folder becomes a project under its own name (a name already taken by another project gets `-2`, `-3`…, so a second folder never joins an existing project silently), set up as the setup check's yes sets one up (marker, library project, the app's project choice), and is shown. A folder already in a project is simply selected; cancelling the picker changes nothing (ADR-0752 D2). One picker at a time.

3.5 · The first-run guide shows, each time it opens, that Codex waits for the user to trust storytree's hooks, with the one step, until one has run, then that it runs them; with no Codex hooks it says nothing of Codex.

3.7 · Remove, in the app's Projects section or with `storytree project remove <name>`, takes a project added by mistake off this computer's list and frees its folder here (a marker git tracks is left and named); its records stay in the library, and a deliberate join, or adding its folder here again, brings it back as the same project, never a `-2`. An unknown name is refused.

3.6 · Delete, in the app's Projects section or with `storytree project delete <name> --confirm <name>`, drops a project's records for every computer using the library once its name is typed, after saying where they live and who loses them; a snapshot into this computer's backups is taken first unless skipped, and restores it. On POSIX, that snapshot is private from its first write (0700 backup directories, including existing ones, and a new 0600 file), independent of the home permissions or umask. On Windows, owner-only ACLs protect both backup directories (including existing ones) and the exclusively created snapshot before any snapshot bytes, even under permissive inherited permissions; an unrelated non-administrative user cannot read it, and the same user can restore it. Failure to establish privacy or save it leaves the project intact. Its activity lines, transcripts and QA ledger rows go with it, and a computer that had hidden it forgets the name, so a later project of that name starts clean and is shown. Refused for a wrong name, the project in use (on show in the app here, or the one the command's folder belongs to), and while a live session holds a claim in it.

3.8 · The first-run guide explains a Smart App Control block on Windows: that it is Windows 11's reputation check on unsigned apps, where to see whether it is on (Windows Security, App & browser control, Smart App Control), how to turn it off, and what that costs, including that turning it back on needs Windows' April 2026 update or later, and a reset before it

3.9 · Settings → Projects shows and edits the selected project's sentence (what it is, who it is for), saved through the library; a half left empty is unsaid, and a project not in the library is refused
3.11 · The desktop app's first launch asks for no factory folder: setting up the first-run guide makes storytree's own, ~/.storytree/your-factory, when none is chosen, and leaves a chosen one alone
3.12 · The app menu shows your factory folder and imports or switches it with no approval

3.13 · The first-run guide offers to connect each coding agent this computer runs that is not yet connected, one Connect each, and to add a project through the same folder picker as New project…; opening it connects and adds nothing, and with no agent found it says how to get one (ADR-1162 D3).

3.14 · Every failure the setup and project screens catch (Help, its guide, license and feedback, and the app menu's Projects section) is written to the console, so app.log, with what failed and its error, and is still said where it happens.
3.15 · The first-run guide's troubleshooting is for the platform it runs on

3.16 · Before a Connect is pressed, the guide says what connecting means: storytree's hooks send each session's transcript, and the code the agent reads in it, into the library; the scrub of secrets is best-effort; raw records are kept 180 days
3.17 · Add project sets up a folder whose marker names a project this library lacks, and says so
3.18 · The first-run guide says, before a project is added, which languages the map reads, from the code survey's list, and that a project in another language shows only what its agent plans
3.19 · The app's Add project, on a picked folder whose code is only in languages the map cannot read, says the sentence set_up_project says (6.115) in its reply

capabilities.title: 4 · Read the license
capabilities.description:
The license travels with the installed product and is available without visiting the source repository. The user can open it from the same help surface they use after installation.

As built: the desktop build copies the repository LICENSE and both Windows distribution paths carry it at resources/LICENSE. Help → License reads that resource and displays it inside the app without network access or a source checkout. Each open reads the current installation’s file; a failed read offers retry. The Windows installer check compares the NSIS-installed and arm64 unpacked resources with the repository license.

Evidence: packages/app-setup/evidence/help/README.md. Unit tests and headless Chromium cover offline reading, a replaced resource and retry; a real installed-release update and arm64 installation remain Windows acceptance work.

contracts.title: 4.1 · An installed user can open the shipped Apache License 2.0 while offline, without a source checkout.
4.2 · Every offered distribution path carries that same license, and the help action still opens it after an update.

capabilities.title: 5 · Send feedback
capabilities.description:
A button in the app lets the user describe a problem or suggestion and opens it as a draft GitHub issue on storytree's repository. They see what they are sending and submit it themselves.

As built: Help → Send feedback provides editable title and message fields and an explicit Open GitHub draft action. The package constructs https://github.com/storytree-ai/storytree/issues/new with only those two user-authored fields; the desktop carries the OS external-browser action. It attaches no project contents, paths, transcripts or logs. A failed handoff preserves the message and offers retry or copy, with an explicit copy failure and selectable original text. Success says “Opened a draft”, leaving GitHub submission to the user. Closing help sends nothing.

Evidence: packages/app-setup/evidence/help/README.md. Fake-opener tests and the actual desktop renderer cover no-project and both-forest access, cancellation, editing, retry, copy, exact payloads and honest success status. No issue was submitted by the checks.

2026-10-06 foundation: the view additionally accepts an optional feedbackIdentity bridge. Only entering Send feedback queries its status. Sign-in remains optional, and a separate Add account to message action inserts the verified email and portable Storytree ID into the editable message, which the user may remove before copy or browser handoff. No bridge is wired into the shipped desktop yet; that integration is parked on the identity arc. Local contract 5.5 and Chromium fixture captures: packages/app-setup/evidence/identity/README.md. These are not live provider or deployed desktop acceptance.

contracts.title: 5.1 · Send feedback is available both with no project and while viewing either project's forest, and opens a prefilled draft GitHub issue on storytree-ai/storytree in the browser.
5.2 · Before submission the user can review and edit their message; the action sends no project contents, paths, transcripts or logs automatically.
5.3 · Failure to open the browser draft offers a retry or a copy of the prepared text.
5.4 · After opening the draft the app says it opened a draft, never that feedback was received.
5.5 · Feedback offers optional sign-in only when requested, adds the verified Storytree account only to the editable message on request, and remains usable signed out or after a sign-in failure.

5.6 · The shipped desktop offers sign-in for feedback only when its build carries a public WorkOS client ID and an HTTPS identity endpoint; it signs in through the system browser and the storytree-auth callback, and no token reaches the page.

parkedOn.title: Identity for a first Storytree user

capabilities.title: 13 · Consent and allowed milestones
capabilities.description: Persist the user's default-off choice, anonymous installation UUID and strict event policy in Setup's journey events (packages/app-setup/src/journey-events).

contracts.title: 13.1 · A new installation records no milestone while sharing is undecided or declined; explicit consent persists across reopen and enables only later milestones.
13.2 · Only the eight approved milestone kinds and their validated safe fields can enter the queue; unknown events, arbitrary properties and free-text error content are refused.
13.3 · An installation keeps its generated anonymous UUID across reopen and uses that UUID for its milestone identity; provider identifiers and tokens are never taken as analytics identity.
13.4 · Successful project creation and landed-increment closure record their milestones only while sharing is on; cancelled setup and other closure outcomes record none.
13.5 · A hooks-verified milestone is emitted only after the setup tool's existing four-hook check verifies the current session; incomplete or another session's evidence emits none.

capabilities.title: 14 · PostHog delivery
capabilities.description: Deliver sanitized milestones through the Node client to PostHog US (ADR-0908) with a small durable offline queue and bounded CLI shutdown.

contracts.title: 14.1 · A consented milestone survives offline failure and process restart in a bounded disk queue; a successful retry removes only the delivered entries.
14.2 · Delivery uses PostHog US (ADR-0908) through the Node transport with IP/GeoIP collection disabled and no added person properties; missing configuration performs no network request.
14.3 · Turning sharing off clears queued milestones and blocks subsequent network requests, including another client's pending flush; CLI shutdown awaits a bounded flush.

14.4 · A shipped build is stamped at build time with only PostHog's public project token, which makes sharing available with its retention and deletion contact; a private key refuses the build, and an unstamped copy offers no sharing.

capabilities.title: 15 · Sharing controls
capabilities.description: Offer an explicit first-launch choice and an always-visible settings off switch through a story-owned surface.

contracts.title: 15.1 · First launch offers an explicit consent choice with no preselected opt-in; unavailable live configuration is shown as unavailable and choosing decline leaves sharing off.
15.2 · The settings surface always exposes the sharing state and off control; using the control persists off before acknowledging it and shows how to request deletion.

15.3 · The CLI offers status, on, off and delete-request through the same persisted controls; incomplete configuration refuses on, and each invocation waits for its bounded flush without printing private authorization.
15.4 · The first launch's consent marks itself with the surface id it declares, as an overlay, so feedback sent over it names it; the Sharing tab's panel carries no mark of its own

capabilities.title: 16 · Requested event deletion
capabilities.description: Let a user identify the events to erase and let an authorized administrative caller request their removal without distributing the private deletion key.

contracts.title: 16.1 · Requesting deletion turns sharing off, clears pending events and presents the installation identifier with the configured deletion contact without claiming remote deletion completed.
16.2 · An authorized administrative deletion call targets the requested person's events in PostHog US (ADR-0908); missing authorization sends nothing and responses never disclose the private key.

capabilities.title: 11 · Pipeline wiring
capabilities.description: At setup, or when a project adopts a pipeline, the agent wires the project's tests, and the jobs the parts it has on contribute, into the user's CI through `wire_pipeline`, and proposes branch protection for the user to approve.

contracts.title: 11.1 · In a GitHub project, `wire_pipeline` writes storytree's workflow: on every pull request and push to main it runs the project's install and test commands on each system the user chose
11.2 · In a project not on GitHub, `wire_pipeline` writes nothing and answers with the commands to add to the pipeline the user has
11.3 · `wire_pipeline` proposes branch protection (merge only what CI verified) as a command for the user to approve, and never changes a repository setting itself

11.5 · When GitHub refuses protection on the repository's plan (a free private repository), wire_pipeline offers merging only after every check passes instead of a command that would fail, and only reads the setting

11.6 · In a project that imports a folder recorded by repository and commit, `wire_pipeline`'s pipeline fetches it at that commit into the place beside the checkout where the folder sits, and installs its own dependencies, before the project's install and tests
11.7 · An import recorded with no repository is named by `wire_pipeline` as one CI cannot fetch, with what the user can do about it
11.8 · A contributed job that asks for the history is checked out with origin/main, so a check it runs can compare the change with it

11.9 · wire_pipeline writes, lists and proposes as status checks only the jobs the parts the host mounts contribute, a factory plugin's among them, each from storytree's source at the user's release: with the part not mounted its pipeline has no such job and its branch protection names no such status

11.10 · The workflow wire_pipeline writes runs with read-only repository permissions, keeps no checkout credentials, uses every action at a pinned commit, and takes storytree's source at the full commit of the user's release

11.11 · In a Python project, or one importing a Python folder, wire_pipeline's test job sets up Python and uv at pinned commits, and Poetry where a poetry.lock is, before its install and tests; an imported Python folder's own dependencies are installed by its uv.lock or poetry.lock
11.12 · When the test command runs pytest without -rA, wire_pipeline says CI health cannot credit its numbered tests and to wire it again with -rA

capabilities.title: 6 · Make a folder a project
capabilities.description: After the user says yes, a folder becomes a storytree project: the one check that refuses a folder already part of a project or a second trunk, the project opened (and its library seeded with the starter pack the first time), the folder recorded and approved as this machine's trunk, the marker left, and the app's choice recorded. Joining an existing project from another machine's checkout is the same step on purpose. Reading which project a folder belongs to stays with the hooks, in project routing.

contracts.title: 6.1 · A project name the library would refuse is refused when setting a folder up, and nothing is written.

6.2 · A folder that is a project's trunk, is inside one, is a git worktree of one, or holds one is refused when set up as another project, even with its marker gone, and nothing is written (ADR-0757 D3).
6.3 · A second folder for a project that already has a trunk on this machine is refused, joining or not, saying to work in a git worktree of the trunk; the trunk keeps routing (ADR-0757 D1, D3).

6.4 · A new folder given an existing project's name is refused unless it joins on purpose, on any machine, and the refusal suggests the first name no project has (name-2, name-3…); a matching folder name never joins (ADR-0757 D3, D4).

6.5 · A machine with no trunk for an existing project adds its checkout only on purpose (join), after which a git worktree of that checkout routes to the project, one project shared by both machines; joining a project that does not exist is refused (ADR-0757 D2, D4).

6.6 · A trunk whose folder is gone from this machine (moved or deleted) is forgotten when the project is set up or joined; a moved folder is never adopted on sight and reaches its project only once joined on purpose (ADR-0942 D4). A folder still there keeps its trunk, marker or not (6.2).

6.7 · Setting a new project up gives its factory the bare bones, no role, check or note; each part left out is taken in by its title with the notes it links, and taking every one gives every starter role (orchestrator, librarian, change-reviewer, explorer, story-author, frontend-builder, blind-reviewer, corpus-investigator), the six test-quality checks a review's brief lists, and the notes they stand on; the product holds no copy of its own, and joining it from another machine, or setting it up again after a failed try, adds none
6.8 · Setting a folder up as project "site" leaves a marker naming "site" and its database's identity, and the project's library exists

6.9 · Taking a newer starter pack adds what the library lacks and replaces only the pack records its user has not edited; an edited one is left and named with the newer text beside it; a product project holding no copy takes it into its factory

6.10 · A folder in no git repository gets one: makeRepository runs git init and commits the project's .storytree folder (its marker and .gitignore), says it made one, already had one, or could not (git missing); with no git identity it keeps the repository with that folder staged, and firstCommit makes that first commit once git has one, as it does for an older setup's root .storytree.json staged alone; it never fails the setup
6.11 · Setting a new project up finds the user's factory by its mark, or makes it, and names it, holding no copy of the starter pack; a join makes none
6.12 · Moving an existing project onto the user's factory drops its unedited copies the factory holds and keeps every record it edited or added

6.13 · Setting a folder up leaves its marker at .storytree/project.json, none at the root, and a .storytree/.gitignore holding *.local.json; a .gitignore the folder already has there is kept, the line added once and never doubled
6.14 · Setting up a folder whose marker names a project this library lacks replaces the marker

capabilities.title: 12 · Import an existing project
capabilities.description: A storytree project imports an existing JavaScript or TypeScript project's folder (ADR-0993 D1, D2, D6): the folder is recorded on the project beside its trunk, with its repository and commit when it is a git checkout with a remote, and each package the folder declares (pnpm-workspace.yaml, else package.json workspaces, else the folder itself) becomes a mapped story through the library's mapStories, the only way a story is made mapped. Importing again maps the folder afresh, keeping what stands. The founding choice: the import reads the folder and writes nothing into it; the deliberate act of importing is its approval (ADR-0942). Front doors: storytree import <folder> and the import_project tool.

contracts.title: 12.1 · Importing a folder records it beside the project's trunk, with its repository and commit when it is a git checkout with a remote, and maps one story per package it declares, named as the package names itself, with no capabilities; nothing is written into the folder
12.2 · Importing a folder again adds a story for each new package, retires the stories whose package is gone, and leaves every other mapped story as it stands

12.3 · A folder that does not exist, is nested inside the storytree project without being its own trunk folder, or has no package.json, pyproject.toml, setup.cfg or setup.py at its top is refused, saying why, and nothing is written; the project's own trunk folder may be imported, mapped in place (ADR-1213)

12.4 · Importing a folder again says the commit recorded before and the one recorded now, and the files added, changed and removed between them (nothing when git cannot compare them), and names each explored capability whose covered files are gone, leaving it as it stands
12.5 · A workspace pattern that climbs out of the folder or runs past the matching limits is refused, saying why, and nothing is written; any '*' pattern is matched in time linear in the folder name

12.6 · A folder with pyproject.toml, setup.cfg or setup.py and no package.json imports as Python packages: a uv workspace's members less its exclude (its root too when it is a project), else the root and its Poetry path dependencies inside the folder, else one package; each named as its manifest names it, else by its folder
12.7 · import_project's refusal of a folder with no package to import names the languages the map reads, and, when the folder holds code in others, names those and what still works

stories.title: Mick's dev loop
stories.description: A session developing storytree gets the personal half of its dev loop from Mick's factory: the guidance build and check, the gate steps for plan edges, owner-applied folders and the risk line, the library tools, the lag instruments, the evidence sweep, the scripts that carry the repository to a new one, the coverage survey and test ratio, the heavy-run lock storytree's pnpm test and pnpm gate hold, and code review: the change-reviewer's brief and the QA ledger of what each review finds, the review loop's bound, graduation, risk reading, the mutation report and the verified test run, with the habits card's red, green and landed build section (capabilities 14 to 21, moved from storytree's Code review story and packages/quality-assurance, ADR-1209). Its code is the micks-dev-loop plugin in HuaMick/storytree-factory (ADR-1192 D2, ADR-1174), moved there from storytree's packages/dev-loop, which is gone: it reaches storytree only through the checkout it runs in, is added as a part of its own (named in settings, standing in for none of storytree's), and its tests run in the factory, not in storytree's CI. The base half (the scoped test runner, the worktree installer, the merge-queue scripts) is the base dev loop's, and the repository's own checks are storytree's repo-checks.

radius.reason: 0 packages downstream; no audience of its own or downstream, so owner

capabilities.title: 4 · Agent guidance
capabilities.description: Builds CLAUDE.md's generated region, AGENTS.md and the role files from the agent roles in the library, and a SKILL.md for Claude Code and Codex from each process note marked as a skill (ADR-0837), and checks the checked-in copies for drift and size (build-guidance.mjs, guidance.mjs).

contracts.title: 4.1 · The session-orchestrator role becomes CLAUDE.md's generated region and AGENTS.md, and every other role becomes a Claude Code and a Codex role file.
4.2 · The drift check names a stale region, missing, stale and orphaned files, ignoring line endings; a CLAUDE.md without the region markers is refused, naming them.
4.3 · A generated file over its size budget is named with its size and its budget.
4.4 · A process note marked as a skill is written out as a Claude Code and a Codex skill, and drift-checked
4.5 · The drift check fails a branch only on its own drift; a file drifted by another editor's unlanded library edit is named with that editor and does not fail it
4.6 · A skill carries a linked pattern whole where its steps say {{include <id>}}, so editing the pattern and rebuilding changes the skill
4.7 · pnpm build:guidance and pnpm check:guidance run Mick's plugin's guidance build and check verbs, and a run that fails is refused with what it said

capabilities.title: 5 · Library tools
capabilities.description: Reaches storytree's own library from the command line to export its stories and decisions as read-only files, restore a snapshot, record an acceptance run, and fold story text, through the repository's own checks' library server (export-library.mjs, library-export.mjs, restore-library.mjs, record-acceptance.mjs, acceptance-health.mjs, fold-story-text.mjs). Recording each contract's verified health from a test run (check-own-health.mjs, 5.13) and the library server (library-server.mjs, 5.1) moved into Storytree's own repository checks by increment_fc3a008fe1c6.

contracts.title: 5.2 · Exporting writes the stories and decisions out as files and writes nothing to the library.
5.3 · Restore reads the snapshot path whether or not `--project` is given, and with no path prints its usage.

5.5 · An acceptance run's verdict on a contract is minted by its harness from the checks it observed: passing only when it ran checks for the contract and every one passed, failing when any failed, and nothing written when none ran or one was not observed. It is written to the verified column by "acceptance run", with the commit and the evidence path in its note.
5.10 · Export and restore reach the library the library setting names (the app's own, a Postgres address or Cloud SQL), and say which
5.11 · The story-text fold moves each piece into its story's or capability's text in the order written and retires it, lists one with no cover, and leaves no definition that is story prose
5.12 · pnpm library:export, pnpm library:restore and pnpm record:acceptance run Mick's plugin's library-tools verbs with the words given, and a run that fails is refused with what it said

capabilities.title: 7 · The gate
capabilities.description: Mick's checks in storytree's `pnpm gate` (check:guidance, check:plan-edges, check:owner-applies, check:risk), contributed as micks-dev-loop's gateSteps and run while this computer names the plugin, each NOT RUN with its reason when it does not apply. The gate's entry in storytree, its worktree install and its holds, moved to storytree's own repository checks' 8 · Storytree's own test and gate entries with its 7.5 (increment_fc3a008fe1c6).

contracts.title: 7.1 · The gate runs the typecheck and the scoped tests, and marks guidance NOT RUN with its reason, without failing, when no generated guidance changed.
7.2 · When the change scope cannot be read, the gate runs the guidance check rather than assuming nothing changed.

7.23 · A capability depending on another story's capability is refused when the first story's package does not depend on the second's, directly or through other workspace dependencies; pnpm gate checks it against the library (ADR-0840 D2).
7.11 · The gate writes the branch's change its risk line
7.17 · A branch changing a folder the owner applies by hand fails the gate until an open increment's owner wait names that folder; a Markdown-only change leaves the check NOT RUN

capabilities.title: 8 · Lag instruments
capabilities.description: The kept instruments that measure the app's lag (ADR-0836, ADR-1001), so every lane and re-measure compares before and after with the same instrument and the same seed: `pnpm lag:reads` times the page's reads over a throwaway Postgres with added latency per query, and `pnpm lag:desktop` performs the catalogue of named actions (opening the smallest, largest and a named story's island, closing the panel, Library and back, opening a Library note and a session's row, a hover sweep, turning the map in the forest and the Library by a Ctrl+drag, idle) through real input on an instrumented copy of the desktop app, or the desktop page in headless Chromium over the stand-in bridge (`--chromium`, as on the Mint box), and prints each action's response, longest frame, settled time and IPC count against its budget, saying NOT RUN for any it could not perform. With `--against <ref | built app dir>` it measures this checkout's build and the other in alternating rounds on the same seed and says, per action, slower, the same or faster, with any read whose count differs as its own finding. The whole run queues behind the heavy-run lock. On the Mint box, `pnpm lag:box` runs it after merges rather than by hand (ADR-1001 D3): a systemd user timer every 15 minutes measures the newest main against each action's baseline, one bounded run at a time with the merges between skipped; a slowdown counts when a second run agrees, holds the baseline back, and is halved down to the pull request that caused it; the history sits in the storytree-lag database beside the library, which `pnpm lag:box` prints from any machine, and `pnpm lag:box rebaseline` accepts a cost with its reason. Never a gate: nothing of it runs in CI or a pull request's checks. They run from Mick's factory plugin micks-dev-loop (`storytree lag-instruments reads|desktop|box`, which the root scripts call), so only on a computer that names it; the box's timer starts the plugin's lag-box.mjs in its runner checkout.

contracts.title: 8.1 · The read instrument delays every query a page read makes by the added latency and reports the read's query count and median time, the same count with or without the delay
8.2 · Desktop analysis reports the total and function times of a recorded CPU profile, matching each sample to its recorded interval
8.4 · pnpm lag:desktop judges each named action's rounds against its budget in one table, and an action it could not perform reads NOT RUN in the table and the exit code
8.5 · The lag instruments seed one library in named sizes, and two seedings of a size hold the same content and make the same queries per read
8.6 · pnpm lag:desktop starts the app on the seeded library by default and prints one table across the sizes it ran
8.7 · pnpm lag:desktop --against judges each action slower, the same or faster on both builds' medians and most pairs of rounds, and prints a read whose count differs as its own finding
8.8 · pnpm lag:desktop --against performs each action's rounds on the two builds in turn, A, B, A, B, and one build's NOT RUN ends the action on both
8.9 · pnpm lag:desktop --against a ref measures it in a throwaway worktree installed with the repo's provisioning and removed afterwards; a built app folder is used where it is
8.10 · pnpm lag:desktop queues the whole run behind the machine's heavy-run lock
8.11 · The box measures the newest main once it moves, one run at a time, the merges between skipped
8.12 · Each action keeps a baseline; a slowdown counts when a second run agrees; a re-baseline records its reason
8.13 · A slowdown is halved down to the merge that caused it, naming its pull request
8.14 · The history is kept in the library's server and pnpm lag:box prints it per action
8.15 · A run past its limit is stopped, recorded NOT RUN, and the heavy-run lock left free

8.16 · After each measuring run the box writes each budget contract its verified verdict as a lag run, with the commit and the evidence: passing within the margin, failing on a slowdown that reproduced, not re-run when NOT RUN, and never failing on one noisy run

8.17 · pnpm lag:desktop performs a start action as a real start of the page, the kept keys it names forgotten first, timed from the start's navigation with its first progress watched from its first frame
8.18 · pnpm lag:desktop turns the map by a Ctrl+drag from an uncovered point of its canvas, reads its frames, and reads NOT RUN when the map did not turn
8.19 · A lag verdict the box has not renewed for two days reads not re-run: a tick that cannot measure, two days after the last measuring run, marks every budget contract it owns not re-run, once
8.20 · pnpm lag:box install makes each of the box's checkouts locked, and locks one it finds there unlocked, so the session worktree reaper leaves them
8.21 · pnpm lag:desktop ends a round that stalls within its deadline NOT RUN naming the wait it stalled in, writes result.json and stops the app it started
8.22 · pnpm lag:reads, pnpm lag:desktop and pnpm lag:box run Mick's plugin's lag-instruments verbs with the words given after --, and a run that fails is refused with its exit
8.23 · A lag-box tick starts no run while the box's load, with a lag run's added, would reach the pool's saturation point
8.24 · A lag-box tick starts no run while the machine's heavy-run lock is held or a run waits on it

capabilities.title: 10 · Evidence recordings follow their arc
capabilities.description: Finds the evidence on main (a .webm clip, a V8 trace or coverage .json.gz, or a .png screenshot, under an evidence folder) whose arc has closed, maps each through the commits that added or changed it to its pull requests, branches, increments and arcs, and deletes the ones nothing active names and nothing reads, repointing every Markdown link to each at its last copy and linking each from its folder's README by commit (ADR-1123, ADR-1127). It runs from Mick's factory plugin micks-dev-loop (plugins/micks-dev-loop/src/evidence-sweep.mjs in HuaMick/storytree-factory, ADR-1192 D2), as `storytree evidence sweep [--apply]`, which storytree's root `pnpm evidence:sweep` runs where the plugin is named; its tests run there.

contracts.title: 10.1 · A recording goes only when every arc it was made for has closed and nothing active names it
10.2 · A closed arc's screenshot goes as its recordings do, an input stays, and every Markdown link to it is repointed
10.4 · storytree evidence sweep runs Mick's plugin's evidence sweep in the checkout it is called from, and a sweep that fails is refused with what it said
10.3 · A closed increment that names a closed arc's evidence does not keep it; an open one on an active arc still does

capabilities.title: 11 · Carrying the repository to a new one
capabilities.description: Scripts that export storytree's own GitHub repository settings to a file, apply that file to another repository (showing the difference first), copy the current alpha and stable releases byte for byte with a hash check, and build the new repo's starting commit with no history, so the flip to a fresh repo (arc_824a506f2125, process_761459dc626c) is a run of commands, not hand clicks. They run from Mick's factory plugin micks-dev-loop (ADR-1192 D2) as `storytree repo-carry settings|releases|starting-tree -- <words>`, from the storytree checkout, while this computer names the plugin.

contracts.title: 11.1 · Diffing an export against a repo lists every carried setting that differs, and the writes that would close it, without writing
11.2 · The release copy fails when a copied asset's hash differs from its source's
11.3 · the starting commit is an orphan holding the ref's tree, option b without the evidence folders except a set code reads
11.4 · storytree repo-carry settings, releases and starting-tree run Mick's plugin's repo-carry scripts with the words given after --, and a run that fails is refused with its exit

capabilities.title: 13 · Heavy runs, coverage and the test ratio
capabilities.description: The machine's heavy-run lock (heavy-lock.mjs), Mick's factory plugin micks-dev-loop's run hold (holds.mjs): while this computer names the plugin, storytree's `pnpm test` and `pnpm gate` take it (storytree's repository checks' 8.3), as the factory's own test run and the plugin's lag and coverage scripts do, so a second heavy run on the machine (a test run, a gate, a browser evidence command through its wrapper) queues behind the first and names who holds it; the coverage survey writes each package's measured coverage map, and the test ratio reports test and implementation lines (`storytree coverage survey` and `storytree coverage ratio`, which `pnpm survey:coverage` and `pnpm test-ratio` run; the browser proofs the survey adds in are recorded by storytree's own repository checks, 6.2). All in the plugin since increment_fc3a008fe1c6 (ADR-1192 D2), which moved the red-run reporter (13.4) to the base dev loop's 4 and storytree's test entry's lists (13.5) to storytree's repository checks' 8. Split from 6 · Running the tests when that moved to the base dev loop (ADR-1192 D1).

contracts.title: 13.1 · A second heavy run, including a browser evidence command, waits for the first and names who holds the lock; a gone holder blocks nothing, and interruption releases the command and its lock.

13.2 · The coverage run records, for each source file of a package, the passing numbered tests of each capability number whose test file executed its functions, times how many of its functions that file ran, in the test's own process or in any process it started, bundled code included through its source map. Story-owned browser proofs preserve their measured contribution across Node regeneration; failed or unexecuted proofs allocate nothing.
13.3 · The test ratio report gives test and implementation code lines per package and overall, counting no blank or comment line and no // inside a string, template or regular expression
13.6 · storytree coverage survey and storytree coverage ratio run Mick's plugin's coverage survey and test ratio in the checkout they are called from, and a survey that fails is refused with its exit
13.7 · The plugin's manifest contributes the heavy-run lock as its run hold: taking it holds the machine's lock, and its release lets it go

13.8 · A run whose scope is files takes one of two light slots, never the heavy-run lock or its queue, so it starts while full runs hold and queue; a third waits for a slot, and a gone slot holder blocks nothing

capabilities.title: 14 · Quality control checks
capabilities.description: A quality control check is one question a reviewer can answer yes or no about a finished change (for example: is any expected value computed the way the code computes it?). Each is its own artifact in the library, of the kind the library declares for it (the library story, Knowledge artifacts), linked to the principle or guardrail note it enforces; the notes stay, carrying the reason for the rule (ADR-0956 D3). This capability gives the checks as one reading, for the change-reviewer and for people, the same from both front doors.

contracts.title: 14.1 · The checks reading gives every live check with its question and, for each note it enforces, that note's id, kind and title; a retired check is not in it.

14.2 · The command line and the agent link's tool give the same checks reading, each through this package's public API; the tool is the one this package registers on the agent link's server, which serves it, and the review loop's tools, for every project, storytree's own or a user's.

14.3 · Quality assurance declares the `quality` verbs the command line mounts: `quality checks` answers with the checks reading, and a verb that needs the ledger is refused when the door hands no server

capabilities.title: 15 · Change review
capabilities.description: The review of one change (one increment's branch) by the `change-reviewer` role, run as an ordinary subagent with a fresh context once the change is green and before the gate (ADR-0956 D1). This capability makes what the reviewer reads, the review brief: the branch's diff against origin/main, the contracts of the capabilities the increment names, and the live checks, with nothing of the implementer's reasoning. And it takes what the reviewer returns: for every check, whether the change trips it and where; for every contract, whether the change does what it says. The role's own text is an agent role in the library, a note, and is not contracted here.

contracts.title: 15.1 · The brief for a change's first review holds the branch's diff against the default branch origin names (origin/main when it names none), every contract of the capabilities its increment names, and every live check with its question, and nothing else: the increment's own body is not in it.

15.2 · A review's return is taken only when it answers every check in its brief (tripped or not, and where tripped: the file, the line and what was found) and every contract in it (met or not, and why not); a return that leaves one unanswered, or answers one the brief did not hold, is refused, naming it, and nothing is recorded.

15.3 · The command line and the agent link's tools issue the same brief and take the same return, each through this package's public API; the brief's tool takes the change's diff, or the worktree to read it from, as an argument, since the agent link's folder is not the branch.

15.4 · A contract the increment rewords through a pending change is in its brief in the pending text, marked pending, and one it retires through a pending change is listed as retired with its reason and is not to be answered; a return that answers a retired one is refused, naming it. Each appears in the brief once: its plan change is not listed again among the pending plan changes, so a return answering it once is taken.
15.5 · The brief lists each contract under its story and capability, so two stories' contracts sharing a number both appear, each with its story
15.6 · The diff read from a worktree holds its uncommitted work too, edits and new files Git does not ignore; a folder whose origin names no default branch is read against its own commit

15.7 · In a repository with no origin/main the brief's diff is read against its local default branch (init.defaultBranch, else main, else master), and the brief names that branch as the repository's own
15.8 · The brief reads the change from the worktree on the branch its increment was claimed on, wherever the brief runs, and is refused naming that branch when no worktree is on it
15.9 · A return names the review it answers, and take refuses one naming another review, such as a return left from an earlier review, recording nothing
15.10 · A plan-only change, whose diff touches no file, gets a brief listing its pending plan changes as the thing under review; one with neither a diff nor a pending change is still refused
15.11 · A low-tier change gets a light pass, judged from its diff alone; medium, high or an unread tier gets the full brief

15.12 · The brief lists each change-triggered guardrail of the stories and capabilities the increment names; the return answers each passed or failed with pictures, and a failed one stands until a later review passes it

15.13 · A return says of each contract whether the change touches it; a touched contract answered met names the test that covers it, or is taken as a hit at the changed line asking for one, and one the change adds or rewords cannot be answered untouched
15.14 · A new test with no saved red run naming it failing is a hit
15.15 · A red run saved in another worktree counts when its commit is in this worktree's history
15.16 · `quality brief` and `take` review a change in a named checkout outside the project, as the owner's factory repo is, and record it in the project's ledger

15.17 · A check that names the projects it applies to is in the brief only of a change in one of those projects; a check that names none is in every project's brief, so a user's project, reading its factory's checks, is not asked storytree's own

15.18 · The brief of a change to a factory plugin's story carries the factory branch's diff and the plugin plan's contracts, refuses to count them met when that branch is unread, and reads the plugin crossed only when no branch carries the change

15.19 · `quality brief --also <folder>`, given once per checkout, lists each outside checkout's diff beside the change's own in one brief, and `quality take --also` runs the graduated checks there too
15.20 · A test a factory worktree's or an --also checkout's diff adds is listed with whether that checkout's saved red runs name it failing, and one none names is a hit
15.21 · A test that only moved or was renumbered is not a new test
15.22 · The brief lists the library records the increment's sessions wrote since claiming it, as part of the change under review

15.23 · A check's answer may name places without tripping it, each with its file, line and what it is; the take keeps them in the return and prints them under their check, and refuses a named place with no file, line or words

15.24 · `quality brief` and `take` run with no --checkout read the factory's worktree on a branch carrying the increment's id as the change's other half, though no capability the increment names is a plugin's, and the brief is refused naming such a branch with no worktree on it

15.25 · A brief whose change spans more than one repository opens with an index of its diffs: one line per repository, naming its checkout, its changed files' count and the brief line its diff starts at; a one-repository brief has none

15.26 · A brief whose contracts would run past what one read shows lists each contract the change leaves untouched in one short line, its id and the start of its title under its capability, with the command that reads it whole; every check, and every contract the change rewords or its diffs name by number, stays whole

capabilities.title: 16 · QA ledger
capabilities.description:
The record of what quality control finds, kept in the library's Postgres (ADR-0956 D4). Every review records, for each check it ran, whether it hit, and for each hit the implementer's answer: fixed, or rejected with a reason. Rows are scoped by check, project and package from the first row, because products differ in shape and a global count hides where a check matters. Its reading gives the counts per check per package, the same from both front doors. It only records: nothing here samples, reduces or retires a check (ADR-0956 D6).

Not settled by this plan (2026-10-10, raised with the dispatching session): where the rows sit inside the library's Postgres, as a record type the library declares, or as this story's own tables reached through the library's connection, as the agent link's activity log is. The contracts hold either way.

contracts.title: 16.1 · Recording a review writes, for each check it ran and each package the change touches, that the check ran there and each hit it made (the file and the line), with the review, the project and the time; a check that ran and did not hit is recorded as ran, and a second connection to the library's Postgres reads the rows back.

16.2 · The implementer's answer is recorded on a hit as fixed, or as rejected with its reason; a rejection with no reason, and an answer to a hit the ledger does not hold, are refused and nothing is written; a hit not yet answered reads unanswered.

16.3 · The ledger's reading gives, for each check and each package of a project, how many reviews ran it, how many hits it made, and those hits by answer (fixed, rejected, unanswered); a check that ran and never hit reads ran with no hits, never absent, and another project's rows are never counted.
16.4 · The command line and the agent link's tool give the same ledger reading, each through this package's public API; the tool is the one this package registers on the agent link's server.
16.5 · The project records this package contributes through its manifest's projectRecords forget a project's ledger runs and hits as it is deleted, and leave another project's

capabilities.title: 17 · Review loop bound
capabilities.description: A review may loop: one iteration is one review and the implementer's answer to each finding. A change is not ready for the gate while a finding stands, which is a hit nobody has answered, or one rejected for a reason the reviewer has not accepted. From the second review on, the brief reads only what changed since the last review (ADR-1120 D2). After three iterations with a finding still standing the loop stops and becomes the owner's question on the owning arc, which the session raises in ADR-0944 D4's order (ADR-1120 D1, replacing ADR-0956 D7's ten). The three are the branch's: an increment landed in several pull requests gets three reviews on each. It is a bound on disagreement, not a checklist to pass: the implementer's reasoned rejection is an answer the reviewer may accept.

contracts.title: 17.1 · A change's standing findings are the hits nobody has answered, the rejections no later review has accepted, and the contracts the latest review found not met; a hit answered fixed, a rejection a later review accepted, or a contract a later review found met, does not stand, and a change with none reads ready for the gate.

17.2 · From a change's second review on, the brief also holds each earlier hit with the implementer's answer to it, and the return must say of each rejection whether the reviewer accepts its reason; a return that leaves a rejection unjudged is refused, naming it, and nothing is recorded.

17.3 · Each review of one change is one iteration: with a finding still standing after the third, a fourth brief is refused, and the refusal names the owning arc and the findings that stand, for the session to raise as an open question there; the refusal itself raises no question and releases no claim, and a change with no finding standing after the third is not refused.
17.4 · The command line and the agent link's tools record the same answer to a hit and give the same standing findings, each through this package's public API.

17.5 · From a change's second review on, a brief read from its worktree holds only the diff since the last review taken, naming that review, while its packages stay the whole change's; once the branch has taken in its default branch since, the brief holds the whole diff again.

17.6 · A change's three reviews are its branch's: a review whose commit its default branch has since taken in (an earlier merged pull request's of the same increment), whose commit the repository does not hold at all (another repository's, as a branch rebuilt in a fresh history finds), or whose commit the branch's own history does not hold (another branch's of the same increment, an earlier lane's), does not count toward the three, while one branch still stops at three
17.7 · A contract finding stands only while the increment still names its contract
17.8 · An accepted rejection is not re-taken by a later review

17.9 · A finding standing only on a line the change's diff does not change does not refuse the fourth brief on its own, so a fourth review judges it; with it still standing after the fourth, the fifth brief is refused

capabilities.title: 18 · Graduation
capabilities.description: Graduating a check moves all of it, or the part of it that is a fixed pattern, from the reviewer to a deterministic check in Graduated checks (capability 22, ADR-0956 D5). The check's record says which part graduated and where it is now enforced; the part that still needs judgement stays with the reviewer. Graduated checks do not reach the library, so this capability runs them on the change under review and records what they find in the QA ledger, under the check each graduated from.

contracts.title: 18.1 · Graduating a check, whole or in part, writes on its record which part graduated and the graduated check that now enforces it, and the checks reading shows both; naming a graduated check that does not exist is refused, and nothing is written.
18.2 · A check graduated whole is no longer in the review brief; one graduated in part stays in it with the graduated part named, so the reviewer judges only the rest.

18.3 · Recording a review also records what the graduated checks (capability 22) find on the same change: each as ran, with each hit, under the check it graduated from, by project and package, marked as the graduated check's and not the reviewer's; the ledger's reading counts them under that check.

capabilities.title: 19 · Risk reading
capabilities.description: Reads a change's risk line (tier, rating, depth, radius, flags, stories) from its diff and the package graph, and each story's standing risk reading from its package's code, deterministically (question_1740edf77e9e, question_0f21964e8ce0).

contracts.title: 19.1 · A change's risk line is read from its diff and the package graph
19.2 · Each story's standing risk reading is read from its package's code and its place in the graph
19.3 · `quality risk` writes an increment's risk line, and `quality story-risks` every story's reading, each run as a write, so its history entries name the session or person who ran it
19.4 · `quality story-risks` writes no history for a story whose reading has not changed since its last run, whatever day it is read

capabilities.title: 20 · Mutation report
capabilities.description: Each change gets a small mutation report (ADR-1153 D1): at most one deliberate break per changed line, about 15 at most, run against only the tests that reach the line's file; arid lines are left out, and each break no test notices is a hit recorded with the review, ranked by what depends on its file. It never blocks a merge.

contracts.title: 20.1 · A change's breaks are at most one per changed source line, about 15 in all spread across them, and none on an arid line: a logging or output call, an upper-case constant's setting, or a line on the arid list

20.2 · Each break runs against only the tests that reach its file; one no test notices survives, ranked by how many files depend on its file, a file no test reaches survives untried, and tests that fail unbroken are left out, a break with none left not run and said so

20.3 · The brief read from a change's worktree carries its mutation report, and taking that review's return records each survivor as a hit found by the mutation report, which the implementer answers like any other

20.4 · A rejected survivor's line joins the arid list and is not offered again, and the rejection stands without a reviewer accepting it, so the report never holds a change back; a report that cannot run says why and never refuses a brief

20.5 · A break its own package's tests miss, or cannot judge because they all fail unbroken, is run against the tests downstream that reach its file before it is called a survivor; one those tests cannot judge either, or the report's time runs out on, is not run, never a survivor
20.6 · A break is caught when a test that passed with nothing broken no longer passes with it planted, so a test failing unbroken leaves out only itself, not the other tests in its file
20.8 · A report never changes the checkout it is given: its breaks are planted in a copy, and a killed report's copy is removed by the next one
20.9 · A killed report's throwaway Postgres is stopped, and its folder removed, by the next report

20.10 · The brief's mutation report also runs on each outside checkout it reads, a factory worktree or an --also checkout, its survivors recorded as hits with the review, or says why it did not run there
20.11 · A line the change adds exactly as a line it deletes, in its own diff or an outside checkout's, gets no break; the lines it edited still do
20.12 · Beside a file's judged breaks, a report names each test file reaching it that it left out for failing with nothing broken

capabilities.title: 21 · Verified test run
capabilities.description: storytree runs a project's test command itself and records the result against the folder's files, so the next role in a user's build loop (the orchestrator after the green builder, the reviewer) reads that run instead of running a slow suite again.

contracts.title: 21.1 · run_tests runs the command in the folder and records its exit code, time and last lines against the folder's files and the command, answering passed or failed with them

21.2 · run_tests with the same command at the same files, committed or not, answers from the recorded run, naming who ran it and when, without running it; an edited or new file, another command, or fresh runs it again
21.3 · run_tests in a folder outside any Git repository is refused, saying why, with nothing run

21.4 · storytree run-tests <command> [--fresh], with no library or MCP server, runs and records the same verified run as run_tests and prints its answer; a run either door recorded at the same files and command is answered by the other without running it; outside a Git repository it is refused, saying why

capabilities.title: 22 · Graduated checks
capabilities.description: Deterministic checks on a change, run from a checkout far more often than CI runs. Each is all of a quality control check, or the part of one that is a fixed pattern, graduated from the reviewer (ADR-0956 D5). Run on the files a branch changes against origin/main, it reports every place a graduated check trips, by the check's name, the file and the line. It reads the checkout alone and records nothing: Graduation (capability 18) runs it and records its hits in the QA ledger. Moved from storytree's Architecture checks story (its capability 4, packages/guardrails) by increment_9a2329880e8b.

contracts.title: 22.1 · Run on a change in a checkout (the files its branch changes against origin/main), each graduated check reports every place it trips, with the check's name, the file and the line (for example a constant asserted equal to itself); a change that trips none reports none, and a tripping line in a file the change does not touch is not reported.
22.2 · It needs no plan, library or running app and writes nothing: it reads the checkout alone, and what it found is its answer, for the caller to record.

capabilities.title: 23 · The check command
capabilities.description: `storytree check`, run in a checkout, runs storytree's package rule and allocation rule (repo-checks' capabilities 9 and 10, imported through the storytree link) and the graduated checks (capability 22) over it and reports every failure plainly, exiting non-zero, or says it passes and exits zero. It reads the checkout alone. The same allocation rule is contributed as a claim check, so a landing on a capability is held while its story package has a source file no numbered test reaches. Moved from storytree's Architecture checks story (its capabilities 3 and 2's claim check, packages/guardrails) by increment_9a2329880e8b; the pipeline job that ran it in a user's CI waits on question_79c1d337e180.

contracts.title: 23.1 · `storytree check` run in a checkout reports every package-rule and allocation failure plainly and exits non-zero; a checkout that keeps both rules prints that it passes and exits zero.
23.2 · It needs no plan, library or running app: it reads the checkout alone.
23.4 · A project whose package depends on an imported app outside it, by link: and deep file paths, passes the check; a rule broken inside the project still fails it
23.5 · `storytree check` reads the frames a checkout declares in its storytree.check.json: a package in a declared frame passes the package rule, one in no story and no declared frame fails it
23.6 · `storytree check` reads the sanctioned edges a checkout declares in its storytree.check.json: a sanctioned story-to-frame edge passes the package rule, an unsanctioned one fails it

23.7 · micks-dev-loop declares the `check` verb the command line mounts: run with no caller, in a folder that is no project, it answers with the check's report and refuses with it when a rule is broken

23.8 · `storytree check` runs the graduated self-equal assertion check on what the branch changes against origin/main: a test asserting an expression equal to itself fails the check, named by file and line; without origin/main it says the check did not run, never that it was kept

23.11 · micks-dev-loop contributes its allocation rule as a claim check: for a capability, the source files of its story's package no numbered test reaches; none for a capability the plan lacks (ADR-1170 D2)

capabilities.title: 24 · The placement report
capabilities.description: Rule 5 of the story rules (the journey principle, ADR-1078), counted at the package level as ADR-1085 D3 narrows it. For each package of a checkout it counts the other packages whose production code imports it, type-only imports included, as the map's code survey reads them. Delivery mechanisms (the front-door frames, and the composition root the checkout declares) and plumbing calls (forwarders the survey detects; build steps and cleanups the checkout declares) are listed but not counted. It says the placement each count implies, and names each package placed differently from today, with the loop a move would make. `storytree check` prints it, and it never fails the check. Its settings live in the checkout's storytree.check.json: the threshold, the composition root, the declared plumbing, and off. Moved from storytree's Architecture checks story (its capability 5, packages/guardrails) by increment_9a2329880e8b.

contracts.title: 24.1 · A package's counted callers are the other packages whose production code imports it, type-only imports included; tests and testing helpers make none
24.2 · The front-door frames' imports and the declared composition root's are listed as delivery mechanisms, not counted
24.3 · A forwarder the code survey detects, and a build step or cleanup storytree.check.json declares, is listed as plumbing by its kind, not counted

24.4 · Each count implies a placement: at or above the threshold its own story, one caller inside that story, none its own story, between them separate ways; a package placed differently from today is named, with the loop moving it would make
24.5 · storytree check prints the placement report and never fails on it; placement off leaves it out

stories.title: Code map
stories.description: An agent or the owner focuses any file, capability, promise or story to read what it depends on and what depends on it, the plan joined with the code survey. Owns packages/map.

radius.reason: 8 packages downstream; invited users, inherited from apps/desktop

capabilities.title: 8 · Code survey
capabilities.description: Surveys story source packages and app frame paths (apps/desktop/src) for file ownership, source line counts and imports. Retains tests with numbered N.M titles and import edges, separately tagged as tests and excluded from source line counts. Ownership follows existing nearest numbered-test reach, execution coverage and type-import rules (8.1, 8.6, 8.7); unmatched files remain unclaimed. Lives in packages/map under ADR-0864; the forest consumes this survey for drawing. Callers may survey the current checkout explicitly. The main default reads immutable Git blobs from fetched origin/main, with shared bounded asynchronous fetches, keeping the last fetched main offline and reporting failure when none exists.
